Improving cotton biomass estimation by assimilating SAR data into a modified crop growth model with simple calibration
abstract: Aboveground biomass density (AGBD) is a key indicator in agricultural systems, directly reflecting crop carbon storage potential and yield levels. The World Food Studies (WOFOST) model is widely used for crop growth simulation due to its process-based interpretability. However, its application is limited by complex calibration demands and struggles with spatial heterogeneity. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an assimilation system that integrates Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data into a modified WOFOST model, which requires simple calibration. WOFOST is run in potential production mode, which assumes ideal conditions to reduce input data requirements. Before assimilation, phenology-related temperature sums are aligned with phenology and meteorological data to match local growth stages. Two quantities are then estimated and updated in the model through data assimilation by minimizing the difference between SAR-derived and simulated AGBD. These quantities are the proposed yield reduction factor, which represents the proportional decrease in potential CO 2 assimilation under stresses, and the initial total dry weight at sowing. Validation experiments were conducted using multi-year cotton datasets from two farms in Georgia, USA, differing in whether irrigation was applied. Compared to WOFOST simulations and evaluated against in situ AGBD measurements, the assimilation results improve agreement and reduce error (approximately 43% RMSE reduction at the rainfed site and 15% at the irrigated site). It also delivers spatial maps of biomass, together with model-derived yield and harvest-index diagnostics, and remains operational under frequent cloud cover where optical observations are sparse. This SAR-based assimilation strategy reduces calibration demands, providing a novel and practical pathway to extend WOFOST applications to diverse agricultural scenarios.

title: Sensitivity of air exchange rate and airflow pattern to incoming wind angle in a naturally ventilated dairy barn under varying convection flow regimes
abstract: The precise determination of Greenhouse gas (GHG) emission is a paramount topic in nowadays research and society. In the case of naturally ventilated dairy barns, on-farm measurements are always accompanied with high uncertainties caused by dynamic weather conditions, animal activities, and the diversity of the barns’ dimensions and geometries. This poses an emerging challenge to mitigate emissions since mitigation measures can only be effective with in-depth knowledge about the gas emission process, ventilation performance, and the airflow patterns. We deployed computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models to investigate the relationship between incoming wind angle and the air exchange rate (AER) of a typical symmetrical dairy barn under three types of convection flow regime. In parallel, the flow pattern at three different heights were compared using the image analysis metric mean square error (MSE). We discovered that for natural convection the AER deviation is around 18% on average for different wind angles. For mixed and force convection, the AER deviation was below 30% for wind angles until 60°. Also, a critical wind angle round 63° was found, from which the wind angle strongly influenced the AER deviation as the forced convection became stronger. The analysis of the MSE values for the considered cases at the three heights showed similar variations in the airflow pattern. In conclusion, considering a wind corridor of up to +/- 60° relative to the crossflow can be considered reasonable for on-farm air exchange rate measurements.

title: Development and multiple cultivation seasons evaluation of a temperature-driven process-based model for tomato growth and yield in greenhouse conditions
abstract: As climate change intensifies, extreme environmental conditions increasingly threaten stable crop production, highlighting the need for reliable greenhouse management and accurate yield prediction. This study developed and evaluated a temperature-driven process-based model to simulate tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum L.) growth and yield under greenhouse conditions in Korea. The model was developed using data from the 2022–2023 season and evaluated using independent datasets from the 2023–2024 and 2024–2025 seasons. The model incorporates key developmental processes, including stem elongation, leaf emergence and leaf defoliation, fruit truss development, and harvest dynamics. It showed strong agreement with observed data for major growth variables, including stem length, leaf emergence, and fruit truss number ( R 2 > 0.96; nRMSE = 5.93–11.83%). For fruit yield, the model successfully reproduced the temporal patterns of cumulative yield across all cultivation seasons, showing strong agreement between observed and predicted values. It also demonstrated acceptable performance based on error metrics ( R 2 = 0.86–0.89; nRMSE = 17.50–22.80%). However, a consistent tendency toward overestimation was observed across cultivation seasons. Photo-physiological analyses, including chlorophyll fluorescence and pigment measurements, were conducted independently to interpret plant responses to environmental variation. Although these variables were not directly included in the model, their relationships with growth and yield helped interpret model uncertainty and potential directions for improvement. Overall, the results demonstrate that a simplified temperature-driven modeling approach can effectively capture major growth and yield dynamics of tomato under greenhouse conditions. The model provides a practical framework for greenhouse crop modeling with reduced input requirements, while highlighting the need to incorporate additional environmental and management factors to further improve prediction accuracy.

Digital Twin of a dual-arm autonomous seeding robot for hydroponic greenhouses
abstract: The technological transfer from industrial automation to agriculture in the last decade has accelerated the adoption of advanced tools for improving efficiency, productivity, and sustainability. Among these innovations, Digital Twin (DT) technology has emerged as a promising paradigm for modeling, monitoring, and analyzing complex agri-robotic processes. This article presents the design, implementation, and experimental validation of a DT for a dual-arm autonomous robot dedicated to the seeding process in hydroponic greenhouses. The system integrates a physical hydroponic environment with a virtual replica built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, enabling simulation-based task testing, trajectory assessment, and hardware-in-the-loop evaluation under controlled geometric and operational conditions. The DT architecture is structured around IoT connectivity using FIWARE components, supporting bidirectional communication between the physical and virtual layers. The dual-arm robot is capable of perception-driven seeding tasks, including planter hole detection, cube positioning, seed collection, and deposition into rock-wool substrates, with collision-free manipulation strategies. The results demonstrate that the DT provides an effective framework for testing control algorithms, refining perception–manipulation strategies, and supporting robust operation under the evaluated greenhouse conditions. The proposed approach represents a step forward in applying DT technology to controlled environment agriculture, offering a basis for future scalable, AI-enhanced robotic systems that can optimize crop establishment and contribute to sustainable food production.

title: Soft semantic grouping and feature clustering for panoptic segmentation of tree crowns and trunks in LiDAR point clouds
Advances in remote sensing techniques for surface soil moisture estimation: A systematic review of recent developments (2019–2024)
abstract: Surface soil moisture (SSM) is a vital variable for irrigation management, estimation of crop water stress, and agricultural drought management. This systematic review integrates recent progress (2019–2024) in remote sensing-based SSM estimation, based on 116 peer-reviewed articles selected using PRISMA guidelines. The review indicates that multi-sensor techniques, integrating optical, radar, and climate information coupled with machine learning (ML) and data assimilation methods, have immensely enhanced the spatial and temporal resolution of SSM products. These developments have brought SSM retrieval within the realm of useful, field-scale application for agricultural water management. Hybrid models and AI-downscaled approaches, in particular, have a very high potential for operational decision-making across varying agro-ecologies. Trends in performance, regional research gaps, and areas for improvement in terms of data coverage, especially for semi-arid and smallholder-dominated landscapes, are also addressed in this review. SWOT analysis of prominent retrieval algorithms identifies their advantages and limitations in application, revealing the compromises between complexity, scalability, and accuracy. Although there has been increasing technical development, with few exceptions, there is no large-scale application in actual irrigation systems. The article ends by placing greater emphasis on enhancing stronger validation protocols, improved application within crop and hydrological models, and region-tailored modifications of retrieval workflows. In the future, new satellite missions and enhanced ground data infrastructure offer opportunities to enhance the contribution of SSM to climate-resilient agriculture. This review offers a timely basis to advance SM monitoring systems that are not only scientifically valid but operationally pertinent to sustainable water management in agriculture.

Modeling PPFD propagation and transmittance in ePAR spectrum for canopy and intra-canopy adaptive greenhouse lighting
abstract: Supplemental light is a fundamental driver of plant growth and a key variable in optimizing crop productivity in controlled environments. Light-emitting diodes (LEDs), operating across distinct spectral channels, are widely adopted for their efficiency and demonstrated benefits. However, conventional top-lighting often produces non-uniform distribution, with excessive interception at the upper canopy and insufficient penetration into lower leaves. Intra-canopy lighting has emerged as a promising solution, yet the absence of rigorous models for spatial and vertical light distribution continues to limit optimization of supplemental lighting. In this study, we present and validate a unified mathematical framework for modeling the propagation and transmittance of photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD, μ mol s −1 m −2 ) across the extended Photosynthetically Active Radiation (ePAR) spectrum (400–750 nm). The model accounts for individual spectral channels (blue, red, far-red, white) and their combinations, simulating three-dimensional spatial distribution and vertical PPFD profiles along tomato plants. Validation with multi-lamp experimental data demonstrated mean percentage errors below 1% in spatial top-canopy PPFD and below 2.5% in vertical PPFD transmittance, across all spectral channels. The proposed algorithm operates with low and linear computational overhead, achieving average execution times of 27 ± 10 μ s per PPFD point, ensuring scalability to large greenhouse systems. The proposed model enables precise PPFD monitoring and provides the basis for advanced supplemental lighting strategies, supporting the integration of real-time digital twins for adaptive light management in smart greenhouse environments.

Adapting SAM with dynamic similarity graphs for few-shot parameter-efficient small dense object detection: A case study of chickpea pods in field conditions
abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) of foundation models for agricultural computer vision tasks remains challenging due to limited training data and complex field conditions. This study introduces a Dynamic Similarity-based Graph Adaptation (DSGA) module to adapt the Segment Anything Model (SAM) under extreme data constraints for precise foreground and instance segmentation of small dense objects in complex agricultural environments. Through dynamic similarity graph construction with a learnable polynomial decay-initialized weight ranking mechanism and adaptive local feature aggregation, DSGA establishes robust spatial and dynamic similarity representation with only 4.00M trainable parameters, which is 4.26% of the original SAM. Integrating this graph-based feature adaptation with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) creates a complementary optimization framework that effectively captures both local and global dependencies in image embeddings while preserving model stability and parameter efficiency. Experimental results on a challenging chickpea pod dataset demonstrated that DSGA with LoRA achieved superior performance across multiple metrics evaluated under 2, 4, 8 and 10 shots, with progressive performance gains as shot count increased. Quantitative metrics showed a 17.31% improvement in Structure-measure and a 62.36% gain in adaptive F-measure compared to the baseline SAM fine-tuning. Comprehensive ablation studies and visualization analyses through Grad-CAM and t-SNE validated the framework's effectiveness in feature discrimination. The proposed adaptation demonstrated practical utility for automated agricultural monitoring applications, achieving accurate pod-counting with an adjusted R-squared of 0.8987 for images with 10 to 120 pods under challenging field conditions.

title: Design and validation of a human-inspired picking motion for tomato harvesting
A comprehensive survey on segmentation-enabled precision agriculture: Methodologies, applications, and the road to agriculture 5.0
abstract: By 2050, global food production must increase by 50%. Accurate farmland mapping is essential to meeting this target, yet the task remains technically challenging. Three persistent problems stand out: small and irregular field boundaries, dynamic crop phenology that alters spectral signatures, and the difficulty of fusing heterogeneous data sources. Existing reviews either address remote sensing broadly or focus on narrow algorithmic categories, leaving a gap in systematic treatment of segmentation-driven precision agriculture. This survey fills that gap by tracing the methodological evolution of farmland boundary extraction from traditional feature engineering to modern deep learning and foundation models, and by demonstrating how precise spatial delineation enables critical downstream applications. We introduce a 4D taxonomy that organizes methods along four dimensions: technical approach, data modality, spatial scale, and application use case. Our analysis covers 117 papers published between 2018 and 2026 across three developmental stages: traditional techniques, deep learning, and foundation models. From this review, three bottlenecks become clear. Even the most advanced models suffer substantial performance degradation in highly fragmented landscapes. Label scarcity remains a pervasive barrier to generalization. The complexity of multimodal data fusion also continues to resist robust solutions. To address these challenges, we outline a forward-looking roadmap built on three emerging paradigms. These include agricultural foundation models for self-supervised representation learning, physics-informed AI for trustworthy predictions, and federated learning for privacy-preserving cross-institutional collaboration. Together, these directions point toward reliable, scalable farmland mapping systems for next-generation precision agriculture.

title: Mapping Alpine pasture biomass and nutritional value from hyperspectral field and spaceborne sensors
abstract: Pastures are important components of Alpine cultural landscapes. However, due to unbalanced grazing pressure and climate change, the quality of pastures is degrading, diminishing their capacity to deliver essential ecosystem services and leading to widespread abandonment. Adaptive grazing management practices can address the challenge of under- or over-exploitation of pasture resources, balancing livestock forage demand and pasture productivity. This study evaluates the capabilities of spaceborne hyperspectral data for mapping pasture productivity and nutritional characteristics (i.e. biomass, protein and fiber content) in mid- to high-elevation Alpine environments. Agronomic and reflectance data (350-2500 nm) were collected in the field across different vegetation phenological stages for 128 pasture samples in two distinct Alpine regions. Field spectra were convoluted to simulate satellite PRISMA hyperspectral and Sentinel-2 multispectral sensor configurations, both used to calibrate and validate Gaussian Process Regression machine learning models. Hyperspectral-based models significantly outperformed multispectral-based ones, with an average R c v 2 improvement of 58.05% and an average R M S E c v reduction of 9.83% ( R c v 2 : 0.67, R M S E c v : 225.79 g m − 2 for AGB; R c v 2 : 0.55, R M S E c v : 1.87 % for CP; R c v 2 : 0.65, R M S E c v : 1.71 % for ADF; R c v 2 : 0.62, R M S E c v : 2.66 % for NDF). The best-performing models were demonstrated on a real PRISMA scene, and the estimations were evaluated against in-situ data, showing overall good agreement (average R 2 of 0.60 and average rRMSE of 11%) and high coherence with spatial patterns induced by pasture composition, grazing and topography. Our results confirm the potential of current (e.g., PRISMA, EnMAP) and upcoming operational hyperspectral missions (e.g., ESA’s CHIME) for regional forage biomass and nutritional quality assessment.

title: Fusion of Litest-HRNet and Skeleton GCN for real-time calf posture monitoring
abstract: Neonatal calves' early daily behaviors are closely related to their health status, serving as crucial early disease indicators. However, in single-calf isolation housing, manual inspection is inefficient, highlighting the need for real-time, non-contact posture monitoring solution for edge devices. To address this need, a lightweight posture monitoring framework for calf-hutch scenarios was proposed. The proposed method was realized by integrating a keypoint estimator and a skeleton-based classifier built upon Lite-est High-Resolution Net (Litest-HRNet). Rapid calf localization was first achieved using the nano-scale lightweight Real-Time Models for Object Detection (RTMDet). Litest-HRNet was then developed by incorporating Dilated Convolution and Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention with coordinated depth–width scaling to improve keypoint regression stability under self-occlusion. Finally, a Skeleton Graph Convolutional Network (Skeleton GCN) with angle-feature enhancement was constructed to explicitly model keypoint topological dependencies for binary classification of standing and lying postures. Experimental results showed that RTMDet-n achieved an Average Precision (AP) of 0.959 with 3.60 G Floating Point Operations (FLOPs). For keypoint detection, Litest-HRNet achieved an AP of 0.9641 and Average Recall (AR) of 0.9701. Compared to the baseline Lite-HRNet, the model reduced FLOPs by 40.2% and Parameters by 43.3%, maintaining a compact size of 3.12 MB and an inference speed of 76.41 Frames Per Second (FPS). An overall accuracy of 90.10% was achieved at an inference speed of 32.7 FPS, demonstrating that the real-time requirements for calf posture estimation were realized. With its non-contact, real-time, and objective characteristics, the proposed method could provide an extensible solution for continuous monitoring of individual calf behaviors.

title: “Please, mind the gap”: A narrative review on digitalization gaps and barriers in the livestock sector
abstract: The livestock sector generates large volumes of data; however, these data remain underutilized. The Data Governance Act, the Data Act of the EU, and recent technological advances, provide an opportunity to automate and improve collection, integration, and use of livestock data. Data spaces, as secure and interoperable environments for data sharing, offer a promising framework to support this transformation. However, this can only be achieved by removing implementation barriers to data sharing and new data generating technologies. The aim of this paper is to provide an overview of key digitalization barriers and gaps in livestock sector. We synthesized existing knowledge across five topics: 1) interoperability, 2) economic viability, 3) technical skills, 4) data privacy and security, and 5) data robustness and quality. Finally, a narrative on how these gaps could be bridged was provided. We argue that bridging these gaps requires a holistic approach combining training, trust building, data governance, and collaboration. EU-level initiatives and projects address some of these areas, but better coordination is needed to maximize impact. The Data Act provides a regulatory foundation for data sharing, yet its limitations, such as its horizontal nature, narrowly defined or unclear terms and exclusion of insights derived from product and related service data, leave critical gaps and may lead to legal disputes. To overcome persistent data lock-in, proactive negotiation, public APIs, and an update on a voluntary industry code of conduct to align with the Data Act are essential for fostering transparency and accelerating adoption of digital solutions.

title: The speed–precision paradox in seeding technology: a system-level review of regime transitions, validation gaps, and energy trade-offs

Semantic metadata extraction from crop model components with large language models to facilitate platform interoperability
abstract: Process-based crop models encapsulate agro-ecosystem knowledge in modular components, yet structural heterogeneity across platforms limits component reuse and demands manual curation of semantic metadata, which is error-prone and time consuming. Here, we present a workflow that leverages large language models (LLMs) to automatically create Crop2ML model specifications by extracting input/output variables specifications and by generating descriptions, from source code written in three different languages among six simulation platforms. Evaluation on eight soil temperature components from six widely used platforms and on 31 various components from three platforms showed F1-Score above 93% for input/output variables extraction. The workflow successfully inferred plausible metadata when documentation was ambiguous or incomplete. These findings demonstrate that LLM-assisted extraction can accelerate the creation of interoperable, semantically rich model documentation while preserving accuracy, thereby lowering the barrier to crop model reuse.

Analytical model of duckfoots draught force prediction based on soil parameters and technical tools, and its validation in laboratory conditions
abstract: The scientific objective of this work was to develop an analytical model for predicting the draught force required to overcome soil resistance by row weeders' duckfoots. The model considered variable duckfoot geometry, dynamic soil effects (i.e., changes in density, moisture, cohesion, and friction under tool loading), and nonlinear soil-implement interactions. The model was validated for three duckfoots with widths of 105 mm, 133 mm, and 202 mm. The tools were mounted on two types of flexible tines: a conventional S tine (stiffness 5.3 kN·m−1) and a Vibro Crop tine (VCO, stiffness 8.3 kN·m−1). The experiments were carried out in a soil bin filled with clay sand with a moisture content of 10% and 14% and a compactness of 486 kPa, using an instrumented measurement setup based on strain-gauge, laser, and optical sensors to acquire draught force, working depth and travel speed at duckfoots depths of 30, 50, and 70 mm and working velocities of 0.84, 1.67, and 2.31 m·s–1. The draught forces were predicted considering optimised values of the soil internal friction, soil–tool friction, and tool setting angles identified from the measurement data. The model showed good agreement with the experimental draught force values. For 10% and 14% soil moisture, the global errors were 18.0% and 24.7%, respectively, and the mean relative error was 0.8% in both cases. The model was validated and confirmed the hypothesis, but it requires further refinement and probabilistic analysis.

title: Planar array radar–capacitive multi-sensor fusion for powdery organic fertilizer flow rate monitoring
Physics-Informed Neural Network methods for predicting plant height development
abstract: ABSTRACT Plant growth is a dynamic process affected by genes and growing environment, with all kinds of interactions between them. These complex relationships make the prediction of plant growth challenging. We propose a hybrid modelling framework that combines a logistic ordinary differential equation model with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network, resulting in a Physics Informed Neural Network (PINN). While PINNs have been widely applied to physical dynamical systems, their use in modelling the dynamics of plant growth systems is still largely unexplored. We illustrate the construction of a PINN on plant height data in wheat and compare its performance with alternative models for longitudinal plant data. All temporal prediction models only require time and temperature as input. Among a set of competing models, our PINN had the lowest average root mean squared error (RMSE) of prediction and the smallest standard deviation across multiple random initialisations. Therefore, we conclude that incorporating biological growth constraints into data-driven growth models can enhance prediction accuracy of longitudinal plant traits. Highlights Integrating plant growth equations into a temporal neural network improves plant height growth prediction over ordinary differential equations and machine learning models, especially when training data are limited.

title: Multi-device RGB image alignment for color-based prediction of soil organic carbon
Corrigendum to “Multi-task geometric regression with agronomic priors for crop row and missing seedling detection in maize-soybean strip intercropping” [Comput. Electron. Agr. 243 (2026) 111383]

Effects of different LED light wavelengths on deep learning-based insect detection in arable crops
abstract: Approaches for automated image-based insect detection are rapidly maturing and becoming a reality for commercial use. However, complex image backgrounds, lighting variations and high variability between different insects’ physical appearance can reduce detection accuracy. Integrating artificial LED lighting into the image acquisition process can enhance the visibility of key insect morphological features, particularly in field applications, thereby improving feature extraction and overall detection performance of machine learning models. Achieving this requires the identification of light wavelengths that best reveal important insect characteristics, such as pigmentation, body patterns, and nanoscale-structural reflections, for more effective discrimination analysis and model training. We investigated the effect of five different LED wavelengths (red (600–700 nm), blue (400–500 nm), white (400–700 nm), UVA (315–400 nm) and a composite mixture of Blue, White, and red (BWR)) on insect identification and on the performance of deep learning-based detection methods in comparison with images taken in natural field conditions. Images of Colorado potato beetle on potato plants and ladybirds and aphids on potato, faba bean and sugar beet were collected with images comprising: (i) simple scenes containing a single insect and (ii) complex multi-class image scenes, with multiple insect individuals on a single image. Using the pre-processed datasets, two deep learning models, YOLOv11 and Swin transformer, were trained and evaluated. Results demonstrate promising potential on multi-class insect datasets, with the blue LED achieving the best detection performance (mAP@50 of 94.5 %) for adult ladybirds. Meanwhile, the composite mixture (BWR) produced the highest performance for both adult and larval Colorado potato beetles, with mAP@50 scores of 96.7 % and 94.4 %, respectively. The red LED performed best for pre-adult stages of ladybirds (84.2 % for eggs, 87.9 % for larvae and 95.3 % for pupae) and for eggs of Colorado potato beetles (88.0 %). For aphid detection, white LED light showed promising performance, achieving mAP@50 of 91.2 %, while the baseline outdoor imaging achieved an mAP@50 of 50.7 %. These results demonstrate that LED lighting enables better model learning and discrimination between different insect species and life stages. The use of LED lights demonstrates strong potential to improve model performance without increasing its architectural computational complexity, thereby facilitating future on-farm deployment of targeted pest management solutions.

title: A multirobot system for autonomous crop field scouting: System integration and demonstration
abstract: This paper introduces an integrated system for autonomous crop field scouting, which incorporates novel algorithms for crop row identification and multirobot task distribution. The system utilizes a flexible team of aerial and ground robots, coordinated by a central computer that manages both the user interface and the back-end software that handles crop row detection and task allocation algorithms. The user interface allows users to initiate the scouting process by selecting target areas on an aerial map and monitor and control the process in real time. Autonomous crop row detection, given aerial images of the target field, is realized via GIS-based autonomous geo-coordinate generation. This information is then inputted into the task allocation algorithms, which determine the number and types of robots and assign them to specific locations to cover the field optimally. The adaptable architecture accommodates different types and numbers of robots to scale to farms of varying sizes. Simulations and field tests were performed to validate system-level integration.

title: Multidepth soil sensing with an embedded hydrothermal stress index captures stratified stability in hardpan-limited tropical spodosol oil palm systems
Optimized ensemble learning frameworks for early grain yield prediction in winter wheat using static and multitemporal multispectral UAV data
abstract: A stacked ensemble learning framework was developed leveraging the large-scale spatial and temporal diversity in a winter wheat breeding program. Multispectral data were collected from 1098 plots comprising 586 genetically diverse advanced breeding lines at tillering, stem elongation, reproductive, early grain filling, mid grain filling, and late dough stages. Raw spectral information, 28 vegetation indices and 16 grey-level co-occurrence matrices were used– both individually and in combination –to train five machine learning algorithms– elastic net , support vector regression , k-nearest neighbours , random forest , and extreme gradient boosting . Static and temporal models were trained for spatial interpolation and genetic extrapolation, followed by internal and external validation. Multispectral features showed stage-specific discriminatory power for separating yield groups, peaking between the reproductive and mid grain filling stages. Classification was limited by overlap between medium- and high-yielding groups. Models integrating multispectral data across growth stages outperformed all other strategies. Elastic net performed best overall, while support vector regression showed the most consistent ranking. Base learners achieved average prediction accuracy of 55.85 % and 46.00 %, with AUC values of 0.73 and 0.66 for internal and external validation, respectively. Selected base-learners were used for stacked elastic net ensemble learning, which increased overall prediction (∼18 %) and classification (∼7 %) accuracies, while reducing errors (∼10 %). These improvements were primarily attributed to reduced bias. Overall, this study presents a scalable machine learning framework trained and validated on an operational breeding program for data-driven UAV-assisted early generation selection, providing a methodological reference for future research and deployment.

title: Color-distance triggering endogenous actuation variable-structure soft grippers with intake-deflation mechanism in finger cups
Pay more attention to electron transfer in agricultural soils
Advancing digital agri-food systems through integrated AI, robotics, IoT, and blockchain with a bibliometric analysis
abstract: Digital Agri-Food Systems (DAFS) are transforming agriculture by combining digital and intelligent technologies to enhance automation, traceability, and data-driven decisions. This study evaluates technical advancements in DAFS by examining 332 peer-reviewed articles retrieved from Scopus. Using a hybrid evidence-synthesis approach that integrates Systematic Mapping and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA), it enables wide theme coverage requiring thorough screening, explicit inclusion criteria, and repeatability. The study identifies dominant research trajectories, methodological trends, and cross-domain technological interactions spanning crop production, livestock systems, food safety, and supply chain management. The findings show a marked transition toward hybrid intelligent frameworks that merge multimodal sensing with advanced analytical models for real-time crop monitoring, early disease detection, yield forecasting, autonomous robotics, and verifiable supply chain traceability. Internet of Things (IoT) sensor networks and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based imaging continue to strengthen precision agriculture practices, while blockchain-enabled systems support transparency, trust, and fraud prevention. Additionally, bibliometric analysis reveals strong international collaboration clusters and rapidly expanding research in precision agriculture, agricultural robotics, and intelligent supply chains. Key challenges persist, such as limited datasets, inconsistent validation, high computational costs, and insufficient focus on cybersecurity. The study shows that advancing DAFS requires scalable, unified architectures linking artificial intelligence (AI)-driven decision tools, interoperable IoT systems, and secure blockchain technologies. The integration is essential for building resilient, efficient, and sustainability-driven agri-food systems.

AI-enabled electromagnetic sensor architecture for precision welfare monitoring in small ruminant production systems
abstract: Climate change and increasing heat stress present growing challenges for the welfare and productivity of small ruminants raised in arid and hot environments. In many production systems, animal health and welfare are still assessed primarily through visual observation, which may delay the detection of subtle physiological or behavioural changes associated with emerging welfare risks. Recent developments in precision livestock farming offer new possibilities for continuous and objective monitoring of animal conditions through advanced sensing technologies. This review explores recent progress in electromagnetic sensing technologies and their integration with artificial intelligence (AI) for monitoring animal welfare in small ruminant production systems. A literature search was conducted using the Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases, focusing mainly on studies published over the past decade related to sensor-based livestock monitoring, electromagnetic sensing approaches, and AI-supported welfare assessment. Studies examining physiological, behavioural, or environmental indicators relevant to livestock welfare were considered. Recent studies indicate that electromagnetic sensing technologies—including microwave antennas, radar-based monitoring systems, metamaterial sensors, and dielectric sensing devices—can detect a range of welfare-related indicators such as respiration patterns, locomotor activity, and hydration status. When combined with machine-learning algorithms, these systems enable the interpretation of complex data streams and support more proactive approaches to welfare management. Based on the reviewed literature, this paper proposes a conceptual framework that integrates three key monitoring modules thermal comfort, locomotor stability, and hydration balance to illustrate how multi-sensor data can be analyzed through AI-driven approaches in small-ruminant production systems under arid climatic conditions. While these technologies show considerable promise, practical challenges remain, including sensor robustness in farm environments, economic feasibility, and the need for appropriate farmer training. Further research is therefore required to evaluate integrated sensor–AI systems under commercial farming conditions and to develop scalable decision-support tools for precision livestock management. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first reviews to specifically focus on the integration of electromagnetic sensing technologies and artificial intelligence for welfare monitoring in small ruminants under arid climatic conditions.

title: A method for quantifying feeding behavior of grass carp in outdoor ponds with complex backgrounds
Estimating grass-clover mixtures quality using field spectroradiometry and stacking-based ensemble learning models
abstract: In this study, we designed a stacking ensemble machine learning method for accurate estimation of grass-clover biomass quality from high-resolution hyperspectral field data. Basic learners were support vector machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), random forest (RF), decision tree (DT), partial least square regress (PLS), shallow artificial- (ANN) and deep multi-layer perceptron (MLPs) neural networks. Three meta learners in the second layer were RF (stackingRF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (stackingXGB), and CatBoost (stackingCat). We used 6 different datasets for the estimation, including the raw spectral reflectance, its 1 st and 2 nd derivatives, and their Standard Normal Variate (SNV). Quality indices were crude ash, crude protein, crude fat, crude fiber, neutral detergent fiber (NDF), acid detergent fiber (ADF), water-soluble carbohydrates (WSC), sugar, and fructans. The results showed that spectral feature selection by the PLS was useful in preprocessing. All machine learning methods predicted well quality from the raw reflectance, with PLS performing best (R 2 = 0.64–0.87) for all indices except crude ash. The stacked ensemble learning benefited the predictions, especially with stackingRF and stackingCat as meta learners (R2 increased by 2–8 % compared with the average of the four best machine learning algorithms in the first layer). SNV generally performed better than the original reflectance across most datasets. In particular, SNV applied to the 2nd derivative, combined with either PLS or StackingRF, yielded the best predictions for carbohydrates (sugar, fructans, WSC) and fiber (crude fiber, NDF, ADF), achieving the highest R 2 values (0.74–0.87) and the lowest nRMSE (5–15 %) among all pre‑processing options. The red‑edge region (700–780 nm) is the most important for all quality indices, except for ADF. This is among the first studies to systematically evaluate stacking ensemble learning, using the outputs of multiple machine‑learning algorithms as inputs, for predicting biomass quality and supporting field management in complex grass–clover mixtures. PLS‑based feature selection combined with stacking ensemble learning on second‑derivative SNV spectra appears particularly promising and warrants testing at larger spatial and temporal scales.

Evaluation of relative grazing intensity based on UAV aerial photography and trajectory tracking technology—a case study of a desert steppe household pasture
abstract: Non-uniform livestock utilization in household pastures is important for understanding grassland growth status and grassland utilization management. However, traditional relative grazing intensity (RGI) evaluation methods are often labor-intensive and limited in their ability to capture fine-scale spatial patterns of livestock utilization, which constrains the characterization of spatiotemporal variation in grassland use. In this study, a desert steppe household pasture in Inner Mongolia, China, was selected as an exploratory integrated framework to analyze cattle herd movement regularities and estimate RGI variation based on unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) photography and trajectory tracking technology. Results showed that: (1) The results from observing trajectory points revealed that cattle herds’ activity within the household pasture is non-uniform. Specifically, the density of trajectory points in densely populated areas is 16 times greater than that in sparsely populated areas; (2) UAV survey not only has high accuracy in cattle population observation (with R 2 and RMSE of 0.83 and 22.56 sheep unit /ha respectively, compared to ground-based observation), but also reflects the spatial activity regularities of the herd. The distribution area of the cattle herd shows a trend of first increasing and then decreasing as the distance to the livestock enclosure increases (P < 0.001); (3) Compared with the traditional method, which divides the livestock population by the area, the spatial and temporal distribution of RGI based on UAV photography and trajectory points shows high consistency (with R 2 ranging from 0.927 to 0.984, compared to ground-based observation), and it can describe the heterogeneity of RGI in more detail; (4) From May to July, the cumulative RGI in pasture showed a trend of gradually decreasing from the northwest and northeast to central area. Our results indicated that, compared with traditional field-based monitoring approaches, the method based on UAV aerial photography and trajectory tracking technology at the pasture scale was less labor-intensive and more time-efficient, while enabling a more detailed characterization of the heterogeneity in RGI caused by non-uniform livestock utilization. As an exploratory case study, this framework shows potential for improving the assessment of spatial heterogeneity associated with non-uniform livestock utilization.

title: Deep learning-based keypoint detection for 3D biometric measurement of tuna using underwater stereo vision
abstract: Accurate and scalable estimation of tuna size during transfer and farming operations is essential for stock assessment and management. This study presents a fully automatic processing pipeline that combines deep learning-based keypoint detection with stereoscopic vision geometry to estimate fish length, height, and width from underwater stereoscopic imagery. The system exploits videos acquired while freely swimming fish under real underwater conditions from two different viewpoints: a lateral view, from which length and height are measured, and a ventral view, which provides length and width. Having measurements of individual fish in all three dimensions can significantly improve the accuracy of estimating biomass and schools for large-bodied species. For each view, a Keypoint R-CNN model was trained on heterogeneous datasets of 850 stereo pairs annotated independently by three human operators. To account for annotation variability, per-keypoint normalization constants were computed and used to adapt COCO-style Object Keypoint Similarity (OKS) metrics to this domain. The proposed Keypoint R-CNN system achieved 2D keypoint localization accuracy comparable to human annotators (mean OKS = 0.91). The resulting 3D biometric measurements yielded relative errors of approximately 1%–2% for length-related dimensions and 2%–5% for height and width, within the range observed for inter-annotator variability. Measurement bias remained below 0.2% for all evaluated dimensions, and no systematic over- or under-estimation trends were observed. Automatic and manual size distributions were statistically indistinguishable, while processing throughput was compatible with offline operational analysis requirements. Overall, the proposed approach provides a reliable and scalable foundation for automated 3D size monitoring in tuna aquaculture.

title: TP-Duck: A cage-reared duck behavior recognition model with lightweight interaction mechanism and text prompts

Soybean leaf physicochemical parameter inversion based on radiative transfer model screening constraints and measured-noise enhancement
Optimized design of a hanging-cup planting principle based on pineapple seedlings and spatio-temporal analysis and experimental study of seedling-machine-soil coupled interaction
abstract: To address the scarcity of mechanized transplanting equipment and poor planting quality for pineapples in China, in this paper, we take "Bali" pineapple seedlings as the research object to conduct an optimized design of a hanging-cup planting principle and a study on the "seedling-machine-soil" coupled interaction mechanism. First, through multi-scale seedling dropping experiments, the optimal caliber for the square seedling cup was determined to be 130mm. Based on the principle of a parallel four-bar mechanism, a kinematic model of the planting mechanism was constructed, and a human-computer interactive parameter design platform was developed to optimize key linkage parameters. The optimal spatio-temporal parameters for the duckbill device were innovatively determined (critical opening angle γ=60°, delayed closing angle Δγ=50°, and maximum opening width W=100 mm). Furthermore, a "seedling-machine-soil" bidirectional coupled simulation model, integrating a flexible body seedling model, multi-body dynamics rigid components, and discrete element-based soil particles, was constructed. This model revealed the spatio-temporal interaction mechanism among the duckbill device's motion trajectory, the seedling's release posture, and soil disturbance during the planting process. The simulation results showed that the optimized planting mechanism could achieve a qualified planting rate of 95.2%. Through indoor soil bin tests and field validation trials, the reliability of the simulation model was systematically verified. The field trial results indicated that at an operating speed of 0.66 km/h, the qualified planting rate reached 90.2%, the miss-planting and lodging rates were 5.1% and 4.7%, respectively, and the coefficient of variation for plant spacing was 4.6%. All indicators were significantly better than the preset standards. This study establishes a systematic research and development methodology for pineapple transplanters, encompassing mechanism revelation, parameter optimization, and multi-environment validation, which can provide a theoretical basis and technical support for the development of high-efficiency transplanting equipment for specialty crops.

title: WheatSim: A process-based wheat model linking organ development, plant architecture, and field-scale responses under environmental variability
abstract: Wheat ( Triticum aestivum L.) underpins global food security, yet process-based simulations of wheat growth remain challenging under variable weather and management conditions. Traditional crop growth models (CGMs) mainly aim to reproduce field-scale outcomes but often simplify organ growth dynamics and plant architecture, whereas functional-structural plant models (FSPMs) represent detailed organ-level growth but are typically confined to single stems and vegetative stages. Explicit plant architecture can integrate organ-specific details from FSPMs into the production-oriented framework of CGMs, thereby establishing a computational pathway that links organ-level responses to plant architecture and field-scale functioning. In this study, we developed WheatSim, a new process-based framework that explicitly integrates organ-level morphology and physiology, plant-level architecture, and field-level production. In WheatSim, organs are encapsulated as self-contained modules with organ-specific models for emergence, growth, and senescence, while multiple organs are organized and coordinated through a tiller hierarchy that defines a botanically realistic plant architecture. A representative plant approach is established alongside the hierarchical tillers to provide a simplified averaging bridge from organ-level simulation to field-scale outcomes. WheatSim couples biochemical photosynthesis and stomatal regulation to simulate carbon assimilation and transpiration, and exchanges state variables with external soil and climate modules for interoperable simulations. Across APSIM NextGen field experiments spanning diverse environments, management practices, and stress regimes, WheatSim showed good agreement with observations for both morphological properties (leaf number, tiller population, and leaf area index) and biomass-related properties (aboveground and grain biomass and nitrogen mass), with relative mean absolute errors typically ranging from 0.1 to 0.3. Temporal trends were also reasonably reproduced, as indicated by linear regression slopes between simulated and observed values that were generally close to 1. The combination of explicit plant architecture and organ-specific models also provides a useful basis for interpreting integrated crop responses to interacting environmental drivers in selected field sites. WheatSim therefore provides an effective computational framework to simulate wheat growth across organ, plant, and field levels, and may also inform future development of process-based models for other cereal crops.

Salmonella risk prediction in poultry farms via deep learning image classification Models, Cross-Region Validation, and edge computing
abstract: Salmonella remains a major cause of foodborne illnesses that are commonly associated with the consumption of contaminated poultry products. Therefore, there is a strong emphasis and a crucial need to reduce Salmonella across the farm to fork continuum. However, there are no easy and rapid on-farm prediction tools to estimate if a flock carries Salmonella . In this study, we used deep learning to develop a Salmonella risk classification model for chicken feces. The model was developed using a two-part framework combining deep learning and tree-based classification techniques. In the first stage, deep learning models such as ResNet152, Xception, VGG19, and others were employed to extract high-level features from chicken fecal images. In the second stage, these features were used by decision tree classifiers including Random Forest and Gradient Boosting for binary classification into Salmonella PCR Positive or Negative. The model was developed using fixed train-validation-test splits on two datasets: an American dataset with 720 images from a controlled multi-serovar Salmonella challenge study and African dataset with 4333 publicly available images. This integrated approach achieved up to 85% classification accuracy when validated across geographical regions. The developed framework was integrated into a user-friendly mobile and web application and allows users to custom train the deep learning classifiers to improve the classification of unseen fecal images. Although the model was primarily validated with the same dataset, this proof-of-concept framework can serve as a decision-support tool for Salmonella control and intervention, contributing to enhanced food safety. Overall, the objective of this study is to develop and validate a hybrid AI approach for Salmonella prediction using fecal images, with explicit cross-region evaluation and proof-of-concept deployment applications.

title: MoeBi-ViT: Non-destructive shoot-stage phenotyping of lettuce in plant factory via dual-branch mixture-of-experts network and enhanced segmentation

Visual-language-guided task planning for horticultural robots
abstract: Crop monitoring is essential for precision agriculture, but current systems lack high-level reasoning. We introduce a novel, modular framework that uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to guide robotic task planning by actively querying heterogeneous data sources—including enriched RGB camera feeds and 2D semantic occupancy maps—interleaved with robotic action primitives. We contribute a comprehensive benchmark for short- and long-horizon crop monitoring tasks in monoculture and polyculture environments. Our results show that while zero-shot VLMs perform robustly for short-horizon tasks (achieving 87% success, comparable to human experts), success drops significantly to under 10% for complex long-horizon, multi-target tasks. Despite this decline, task completion rates remain above 76% under noiseless conditions. Critically, the system degrades when relying on noisy semantic maps, demonstrating a key limitation in current VLM context grounding for sustained robotic operations. This work offers a deployable framework and critical insights into VLM capabilities and shortcomings for complex agricultural robotics. Supplementary material: https://kendallkoe.com/Visual-Language-Guided-Task-Planning-for-Horticultural-Robots/ .

title: NearStitch: Robust near-surface image stitching for phenotyping
abstract: High-throughput phenotyping platforms (HTPPs) are widely used for efficient phenotyping. Near-surface image stitching is one key technology required by HTTPs. However, it is challenged by large-distortion, large-parallax, and homogenous features of images, leading to poor alignment, edge distortions, and ghosting. This study developed an artifact-free, robust, and scalable near-surface image stitching algorithm (NearStitch) with a self-constructed dataset (PlantStitch). It is characterized by its hierarchical structure, primarily comprising three modules: layered feature extraction, layered image alignment, and warping and post-processing. The PlantStitch comprises 34,299 images of various crop types, growing stages, and altitudes, collected using field gantry phenotyping and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) platforms. The adjacent and multi-line stitched results showed that NearStitch had fewer artifacts and less distortion than other commercial software and public algorithms. Besides, NearStitch produced Integrated Local Natural Image Quality Evaluator (ILNIQE) scores of 22.97 for the GS3 dataset (gantry-collected soybean images at 3 m) and 23.12 for the GW3 dataset (gantry-collected wheat images at 3 m). Meanwhile, the average angle difference of checkerboard (AADC) values for the GS3 and GW3 datasets were 1.68 and 0.40, respectively. Compared to the six state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, the ILNIQE scores improved by approximately 7 % on average, while the AADC scores showed an average improvement of around 10 %. Additionally, the algorithms are transferable to other image data types, such as multispectral and thermal infrared stitching. The NearStitch algorithm and software are publicly available on GitHub. We believe that the PlantStitch and NearStitch, as common image processing datasets and methods, will support image-based crop stress assessment and variety screening in high-throughput plant phenotyping by enabling reliable near-surface image stitching.

Integrating feature selection and machine learning for nitrogen assessment in grapevine leaves using in-field hyperspectral imaging
abstract: Nitrogen (N) is one of the most critical nutrients in winegrape production, influencing vine vigor, fruit composition, and wine quality. Because soil N availability varies spatially and temporally, accurate estimation of leaf N concentration is essential for optimizing fertilization at the individual plant level. In this study, in-field hyperspectral images (400-1000 nm) were collected from four grapevine cultivars (Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Concord, and Syrah) across two growth stages (bloom and veraison) during the 2022 and 2023 growing seasons at both the leaf and canopy levels. An ensemble feature selection framework was developed to identify the most informative spectral bands for N estimation within individual cultivars, effectively reducing redundancy and selecting compact, physiologically meaningful band combinations spanning the visible, red-edge, and near-infrared regions. At the leaf level, models achieved the highest predictive accuracy for Chardonnay (R^2 = 0.82, RMSE = 0.19 %DW) and Pinot Noir (R^2 = 0.69, RMSE = 0.20 %DW). Canopy-level predictions also performed well, with R^2 values of 0.65, 0.72, and 0.70 for Chardonnay, Concord, and Syrah, respectively. White cultivars exhibited balanced spectral contributions across the visible, red-edge, and near-infrared regions, whereas red cultivars relied more heavily on visible bands due to anthocyanin-chlorophyll interactions. Leaf-level N-sensitive bands selected for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir were successfully transferred to the canopy level, improving or maintaining prediction accuracy across cultivars. These results confirm that ensemble feature selection captures spectrally robust, scale-consistent bands transferable across measurement levels and cultivars, demonstrating the potential of integrating in-field hyperspectral imaging with machine learning for vineyard N status monitoring.

title: Context-aware adaptive pesticide spraying for agricultural robots under changing weather and terrain using Vision–Language Models
abstract: Precision pesticide spraying is essential for optimizing application efficiency and ensuring uniform chemical distribution. Spraying performance is influenced by multiple factors, including environmental conditions such as temperature and wind speed, pesticide type, and the robot's capability to accurately perceive crops and target spray locations. Existing approaches predominantly emphasize crop detection and rely on predefined spraying parameters, whereas human operators dynamically adjust their spraying strategies by considering environmental conditions, region-specific crop characteristics, and the type of pesticide being applied. In this study, we propose a context-aware adaptive spraying framework based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), which enables robots to leverage spatial reasoning and integrate information from multiple sources, including crop type, pesticide type, and weather data, to make adaptive and optimized spraying decisions. Subsequently, a trajectory-tracking controller based on Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is employed to ensure precise navigation and accurate spraying at crop locations. The comparative results demonstrate that the proposed method improves accuracy by at least 30% in detecting crop rows. In addition, the experimental evaluations conducted in two environments further demonstrate the robot's ability to flexibly adjust spraying volume and travel speed, while reducing pesticide drift.

A physics-informed neural network for continuous rice canopy thermal monitoring and forecasting from sparse UAV observations
abstract: Continuous monitoring of canopy temperature (Tc), a key indicator of crop water-heat stress and physiological dynamics, using unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery is inherently limited by temporal discontinuity and the limited physical realism of purely data-driven models. This study develops a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework to transform temporally sparse UAV thermal observations into continuous hourly rice Tc reconstruction and 48 h forecasting products. The model leverages sparse UAV thermal measurements as supervisory signals while integrating them with continuous meteorological forcing and daily UAV-derived crop phenotypic features. Validated through a comprehensive season-long rice field experiment using walk-forward cross-validation, the proposed PINN framework demonstrated superior performance. It achieved R 2 values of 0.92 for reconstruction and 0.90 for forecasting, with RMSE of 0.71 °C and 0.82 °C, respectively. Ablation analysis further showed that crop phenotypic variables contributed more strongly than temporal descriptors, reducing predictive uncertainty by approximately 4.8–14.3 %, while the integration of SEB physical constraints and uncertainty modeling improved R 2 by 8.4–9.5 % and reduced Total STD by 28.4–37.7 %. The model successfully captures diurnal dynamics, spatial variability, and canopy thermal hysteresis while maintaining physical consistency through improved energy closure. This framework bridges sparse aerial observations with continuous physiological monitoring and highlights its potential to support precision irrigation, early stress detection, and high-throughput phenotyping in smart agriculture.

title: Modeling photosynthetically active radiation for crop suitability and yield potential assessment in building-integrated agriculture: a simulation–measurement framework
abstract: As climate change and urbanization intensify, there is an increasing need for computational tools that support crop planning and performance assessment in space-constrained urban environments. This study presents a simulation–measurement framework for modeling Photosynthetically Active Radiation (PAR) to enable quantitative crop suitability assessment and relative yield potential evaluation in building-integrated agriculture (BIA) within high-density tropical cities. The methodology integrates climate-based computational simulation with high-resolution environmental sensing and empirical benchmarking using in-situ PAR measurements collected in Singapore. Model validation demonstrates a strong level of agreement between simulated and measured data (Mean Absolute Error = 164.5 μmol·m⁻ 2 ·s⁻ 1 ), supporting the reliability of the approach as a benchmarking tool. The validated model is applied across multiple spatial scales, including the generation of Singapore’s first country-scale PAR maps based on Typical Meteorological Year (TMY) data, and building-scale analyses that incorporate three-dimensional urban morphology. Crop suitability and relative yield potential are derived by linking simulated light availability to literature-based crop light requirements and optimal production conditions in controlled environment agriculture. Yield indicators are interpreted as comparative performance metrics rather than absolute production forecasts. The proposed framework establishes a multi-scalar, sunlight-informed decision-support tool for crop selection and energy-efficient agricultural system design in complex urban environments.

title: Cattle behavior classification using Hidden Markov Models
abstract: The increasing demand for meat production necessitates more sustainable and data-driven livestock management practices. Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) leverages sensor technologies and computational methods to monitor individual animals, enhancing productivity and welfare. In this study, we use Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) to classify free-range cattle behavior using GPS and tri-axial accelerometer data collected from 22 Angus-based cows over a nine-week winter period in western Montana, USA. Following model validation, HMM-predicted behavioral states were used to examine large-scale behavioral patterns across the entire dataset. The analysis revealed pronounced diurnal activity cycles, temperature-dependent shifts in behavior, and significantly greater nighttime grazing activity during full moon periods. Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) further demonstrated significant interactions between temperature and time of day, showing that cattle increasingly shifted grazing activity toward cooler periods as temperatures increased. These findings provide insight into how environmental conditions influence free-range cattle behavior and demonstrate the value of sensor-based monitoring for precision grazing management. To enable this analysis, we engineered four features; step size, turning angle, and the mean and variance of Signal Vector Magnitude (SVM), and used these in a three-state HMM to classify grazing, resting, and traveling behaviors. Model development was conducted using leave-one-out cross-validation to assess generalizability across individuals, achieving an average classification accuracy of 92.72%. Our findings demonstrate the utility of HMMs as robust, transparent, and computationally efficient tools for cattle behavior classification in extensive rangeland settings. The approach holds promise for real-time PLF applications such as early anomaly detection, resource allocation, and adaptive grazing management.

title: A generic framework for evaluating the effectiveness of bio-stabilization: Integrating data-driven and model-driven approaches

Learning adversarial augmentation policies for robust garlic seedling detection
abstract: Accurate seedling detection during early growth stages is essential for timely replanting and effective crop management in precision agriculture. However, existing studies are mostly evaluated under relatively stable imaging conditions, such as UAV imagery or greenhouse environments, leaving robust detection under severe and spatially heterogeneous illumination in ground-based outdoor monitoring insufficiently explored. In addition, many illumination-robust detection methods rely on additional enhancement or feature-extraction modules, which increase inference-time overhead and are not tailored to seedling detection and downstream missing seedling localization. To address these gaps, we construct a new garlic seedling dataset captured using a ground-based monitoring platform under real outdoor field conditions with highly variable illumination. We further propose an illumination-robust seedling detection framework based on adversarial augmentation policy learning. The proposed method jointly optimizes a stochastic augmentation policy agent and an object detector, enabling the detector to learn robust representations under challenging visual conditions. A structural penalty is introduced to prevent unrealistic distortions while encouraging challenging augmentations during training. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach achieves an AP$_{50}$ of 91.6%, improving the baseline by 0.9 percentage points and outperforming the previous best-performing method by 0.2 percentage points. For downstream missing seedling localization, it achieves 75.0% precision and a 67.0% F1-score, improving the baseline by 4.8 and 2.0 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for practical ground-based agricultural monitoring under complex outdoor lighting conditions without additional inference-time computational overhead.

title: Field-scale assessment of ridging operation quality using UAV LiDAR point clouds
Occlusion-aware pinching point positioning using shoot morphology for robotic summer pruning of kiwifruit
Robust multimodal fusion for terrain perception and autonomous robot navigation in unstructured agricultural environments
abstract: Autonomous navigation of agricultural robots faces persistent challenges in unstructured environments, including canopy occlusion, specular reflections from pooled water, and ridge-induced platform vibrations that cause temporally varying sensor degradation. Existing multimodal systems fail to maintain both reliability and real-time responsiveness, while accurate delineation of safety–critical classes (especially waterlogged zones) and the direct translation of perceptual quality into navigational safety remain key bottlenecks. We present a lightweight real-time adaptive multimodal perception system that establishes a complete perception–planning closed loop. Built on MobileNetV3-U-Net-Lite, the architecture integrates (1) six-channel early RGB–LiDAR fusion for deep cross-modal complementarity from the shallowest layers, (2) stepwise collaborative filtering with learnable anisotropic boundary weights supervised by a composite CE + Dice + boundary loss to handle directional terrain margins and low-frequency safety–critical classes, and (3) a 10-dimensional physical state vector (IMU vibration signatures + RGB illumination descriptors) that drives an MLP-based dynamic modality weighting mechanism reinforced by physical-consistency regularization. The fused output generates a quantitative risk map encoding slope, surface undulation, water-accumulation probability, and vegetation obscuration, which directly feeds the Agri Path planner for risk-guided path refinement and global map accumulation. Deployed on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, the system achieves 47 FPS with 3.4 M parameters and 7.8 W power consumption. On the RELLIS-3D benchmark it attains 62.56 % mIoU, 40.42 % puddle IoU, and boundary F1 scores exceeding all baselines. Field trials at Xihua University demonstrate a 91.7 % improvement in minimum safe distance over the IMU-ablated baseline and reduction of peak yaw-rate to 37.5 % of the control group. These results demonstrate a viable pathway toward physically grounded, temporally adaptive safety navigation: shifting from static precision-centric fusion to physically grounded, temporally adaptive, risk-quantified safety navigation under tight edge-computing constraints. Field validation under dusk post-irrigation conditions confirms system robustness under compound sensor degradation; the proposed mechanisms demonstrate strong potential for transfer to orchards, vegetable fields, and wheat croplands, subject to further validation under full nocturnal and adverse-weather conditions.

Key behavior recognition with tracking for brooding layer breeder chick based on RTM-BHJ
abstract: Monitoring the behavior of layer breeder chicks during the brooding period is critical for evaluating their welfare and health status. However, high chick density, frequent occlusions, and rapid fine-grained movements make automated monitoring challenging. To address these issues, this study introduces RTM-BHJ, a real-time framework for multi-chick monitoring based on RTMDet and SlowFast. The framework integrates a Body–Head Joint (BHJ) detector, the NorFast tracker, which combines NorFair-v2 and FastReID, and a SlowFast-based Tracking-Motivated Behavior Recognition (SF-TMBR) model. The BHJ detector incorporates a novel detection head optimized by DSC, DA-SPP-Lite, and Flash Layer to improve detection accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. For tracking, FastReID extracts discriminative appearance features from a pre-trained model. In addition, the temporal aggregation of detected head features along tracked trajectories enhances feature representation for recognizing key behaviors with rapid motion. Experiments across four chick age groups showed that the proposed framework achieved strong detection and tracking performance, with an mMR −2 of 20.8%, a HOTA score of 66.8%, and 272 identity switches. For behavior recognition, the SF-TMBR model achieved AP scores of 78.3% for preening and 72.1% for pecking, and improved Frame-mAP and Video-mAP by 3.9% and 3.8%, respectively, compared with the original SlowFast network. These results demonstrate that RTM-BHJ provides an effective and practical solution for intelligent monitoring of layer breeder chicks during the brooding period.

title: LEGDeeplab: A lightweight edge-guided model for semantic segmentation of maize leaf rust
A process-based mechanistic modeling framework for soil–plant zinc dynamics and rice zinc biofortification
Estimating plant density of maize across the growing season via dynamic fusion of UAV-based multimodal data
