Digital twins in poultry farming management: A review
abstract: Digital twins, defined as dynamic virtual representations of physical systems, offer potential to facilitate real-time monitoring, improve predictive capabilities, and support data-driven decision-making. The application of digital twins in poultry farming management has attracted increasing attention, however, it remains insufficiently explored, particularly in terms of framework development and layer-wise functionalities. This review presents a comprehensive study of digital twin development and components in poultry farming management, addressing the current lack of structured frameworks and systematic analysis in this domain. In this context, poultry farming management is defined as the strategic planning and implementation of a series of farm operations, including monitoring, detection, and prediction, to enhance production efficiency and achieve economic sustainability. Based on the existing literature, a three-layer digital twin framework is proposed, consisting of a data collection layer, a model layer, and an application layer. Within this framework, farm data are first captured and gathered in the data collection layer, then processed and simulated in the model layer, and finally utilized to support decision-making in the application layer. Through a detailed layer-wise analysis, the study highlights the critical role of model calibration and synchronization in ensuring consistency between physical and virtual systems. While offering promising potential, the adoption of digital twin technology in poultry farming faces several challenges, including challenges in real-world deployment, limited system integration, issues related to data quality and ownership, and insufficient solutions to ensure animal health and welfare. Finally, the study summarizes future research directions for digital twin applications in livestock production systems.

title: A Scalable Pipeline Combining Procedural 3D Graphics and Guided Diffusion for Photorealistic Synthetic Training Data Generation in White Button Mushroom Segmentation
abstract: Industrial mushroom cultivation increasingly relies on computer vision for monitoring and automated harvesting. However, developing accurate detection and segmentation models requires large, precisely annotated datasets that are costly to produce. Synthetic data provides a scalable alternative, yet often lacks sufficient realism to generalize to real-world scenarios. This paper presents a novel workflow that integrates 3D rendering in Blender with a constrained diffusion model to automatically generate high-quality annotated, photorealistic synthetic images of Agaricus Bisporus mushrooms. This approach preserves full control over 3D scene configuration and annotations while achieving photorealism without the need for specialized computer graphics expertise. We release two synthetic datasets (each containing 6000 images depicting over 250k mushroom instances) and evaluate Mask R-CNN models trained on them in a zero-shot setting. When tested on two independent real-world datasets (including a newly collected benchmark), our method achieves state-of-the-art segmentation performance (F1 = 0.859 on M18K), despite using only synthetic training data. Although the approach is demonstrated on Agaricus Bisporus mushrooms, the proposed pipeline can be readily adapted to other mushroom species or to other agricultural domains, such as fruit and leaf detection.

title: Tuning into plant ultrasonics: Can acoustics enable smart agriculture?
abstract: Plant ultrasonic acoustic emissions (UAEs) are low-intensity sound signals that arise primarily from physiological processes associated with transpiration-driven water transport. By monitoring these emissions, researchers and farmers can detect physiological changes related to water/drought stress, heat stress, or disease, allowing timely interventions and optimized resource management. However, substantial variability in UAEs across plant species and environmental conditions, together with limited detection sensitivity and a lack of standardized measurement protocols, present significant challenges for robust interpretation and large scale deployment. Recent advancements in portable sensor technologies and network integration, supported by collaborations between crop physiologists, engineers, and data scientists, aim to address some of these challenges. Standardization efforts and more robust methodologies for data collection and analysis are emerging, alongside innovative applications in precision agriculture. These developments promise to boost crop yields, enhance sustainability, and increase resilience to environmental stressors. In this perspective article, we review the current state of plant acoustics research,critically assess available sensing and analytical approaches, and discuss both their opportunities and limitations. We further argue that targeted research into the biological interpretation of UAEs’ including their potential roles in plant-to-plant and plant–animal interactions, in natural ecosystems as well as in controlled environments like greenhouses and vertical farms, is crucial. Within a smart farming toolkit, plant acoustics may become a complementary tool for applications in agriculture, forestry, plant breeding, and conservation, provided that integration across sensing, data analytics, and agronomic decision-making is achieved.

title: A free-view registration network with geometric generation for unrestricted pig body size measurement
Computational approaches for modelling soil water repellency: A comprehensive review
abstract: Soil water repellency (SWR) is a significant soil constraint in agricultural systems, impacting water infiltration, crop establishment, and productivity, especially in sandy soils. Accurate assessment and prediction of SWR are essential for enhancing soil and water management practices. Traditional measurement techniques, including molarity of ethanol droplet and water drop penetration time tests, provide reliable assessments on point-based samples. However, these methods require significant labour and time inputs to extend SWR assessments to farm and regional scales. Recent computational approaches integrating statistical analysis, remote sensing, machine learning, deep learning, and geospatial techniques have emerged as promising alternatives for SWR assessment and prediction. This study reviews existing computational approaches used for modelling SWR and related soil properties across agricultural systems. It synthesises commonly used data sources, including remote sensing imagery, vegetation indices, climate variables, topographic information, and soil properties, together with preprocessing techniques, modelling methods, and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the review examines the strengths and limitations of existing approaches in terms of prediction accuracy, scalability, spatial–temporal generalisation, and interpretability. Particular attention is given to explainable artificial intelligence techniques for understanding the environmental drivers influencing SWR variability. Based on the reviewed literature, this study identifies existing research gaps and presents future research directions for developing scalable, interpretable, and data-driven computational frameworks for SWR modelling and precision soil management.

title: Label-efficient structure-aware learning framework for wheat tiller density estimation from UAV remote sensing
Performance trade-offs between single-task and multi-task in multi-source prediction of yield and grain protein content in winter wheat
abstract: Early-season prediction of winter wheat yield and grain protein content is essential for guiding fertilizer and irrigation decisions and reducing uncertainty in variable agroecosystems, as yield affects profitability and quality affects market value and nutrition. Although multi-source data and both single-task learning (STL) and multi-task learning (MTL) are widely used for predicting grain yield and quality, the conditions under which each approach performs best remain poorly understood, especially when data availability, noise, and measurement or computational constraints vary. To address this gap, we conducted a three-year field experiment in Henan Province, China, compiling environmental, agronomic, and proximal-sensing variables across five growth stages. Seven subsets were constructed, including environmental, agronomic, sensor, and combined subsets, and STL/MTL variants of Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Transformer, and Random Forest (RF) were benchmarked. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis quantified feature- and stage-level contributions and guided construction of compact Top-K subsets for accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. Multi-source fusion substantially improved accuracy over single-source inputs, with the combined agronomic-sensor subset providing the best performance (yield R 2 = 0.823; GPC R 2 = 0.743). Under the current stage-aggregated multi-source representation, MLPs outperformed Transformers and RFs across configurations, indicating that compact nonlinear models were better suited to the present medium-dimensional tabular setting. MTL provided the greatest benefit with sparse feature sets or imbalanced predictive difficulty, whereas STL performed better when information was abundant and signals were strong. SHAP analysis showed that agronomic and sensor features associated with biomass accumulation, nitrogen status, water availability, and canopy light interception were key drivers of model predictions, particularly during erecting and early grain filling. These findings further show that the value of STL versus MTL depends on data-source composition and information richness, and that SHAP can be used not only for interpretation but also for reduced-feature subset design. Within the present plot-scale setting, this study therefore provides a decision-oriented framework for identifying both accuracy-oriented and efficiency-oriented configurations, with efficiency referring to feature parsimony, reduced input and preprocessing burden, and computational time for winter wheat yield and GPC.

A virtual nozzle model for the DEM-CFD simulation of agricultural spraying processes
abstract: In crop protection, the assessment of innovations such as spot spraying, pulse width modulation or variable rate application requires new test methods. Their dynamic parameters (e. g. on/off, changing volume flow and concentration of active ingredient) raise new questions concerning, for example, lateral distribution, accuracy of spraying or drift measures under a wide range of parameter settings and spraying techniques used. This cannot be answered easily using conventional test methods. For this reason, new approaches are necessary for the assessment and also for a better understanding of the dynamic behaviour during application. Simulation can be a helpful tool for this problem, but it requires a suitable and precise nozzle model. In this paper results from the creation of a virtual flat fan nozzle and its coupled DEM-CFD simulation are presented. Based on measurement data from various test rigs in the laboratory, the behaviour of a real nozzle was analysed in a plane 100 mm below the orifice in order to create a virtual nozzle in MATLAB that does not require iterative calibration of parameters such as the droplet velocity and the angle of flight, as is necessary for the simulation models described to date. This virtual nozzle was used for bidirectional coupled DEM-CFD simulations using Altair EDEM and AcuSolve. In these the movement of the droplets between the virtual nozzle and the target surface and their interaction with the surrounding air were calculated. A validation of the shown approach to create a virtual nozzle model was carried out by comparing the measured lateral volumetric distribution with the distribution in the simulation model for one and five nozzles on a spray boom at two spraying heights. Furthermore, a scenario with a crosswind was simulated as an example application of the virtual nozzle in order to analyse the drift of the spray fan.

Validation of CFD-SAAS, a modeling tool for predicting pesticide spray deposition and drift from air-assisted sprayers in apple orchards
abstract: A computational fluid dynamics (CFD) based computer program, Simulation of Air-Assisted Sprayers (SAAS), was developed to predict pesticide spray deposition and drift risk for conventional and intelligent orchard sprayers under various weather and field conditions. However, the predictive accuracy of SAAS must be validated to ensure reliability. The CFD simulations used to generate the SAAS data (CFD-SAAS) and the direct output of the SAAS were both analyzed. In-field measurements of airborne drift and spray deposition on the canopy and ground from a conventional and intelligent sprayer in an experimental apple orchard were used for the validations. Mass balances of total spray deposition and airborne drift were included in the validation analyses. CFD-SAAS was valid for predicting the deposition on the canopy and ground at specific locations, with average relative errors of 36.4% and 34.4%, respectively. In addition, the model successfully predicted spatial distributions of airborne drift at distances from 3 m to 12 m downwind and heights up to 2 m above the ground with average relative errors of 16.8% and 20.4% for a conventional and intelligent sprayer, respectively. Furthermore, the CFD-SAAS was able to accurately predict the droplet mass balance for the ground deposition at downwind distances up to 48 m for the conventional sprayer and up to 12 m for the intelligent sprayer with an overall relative error of 37.5%.

Systematic review and meta-analysis of adoption, acceptance, and perceptions of precision livestock farming technology
abstract: Digital technologies are increasingly reshaping livestock production systems, with precision livestock farming (PLF) emerging as a key innovation that uses sensor-based monitoring and data analytics to support animal management, welfare oversight, and decision-making on farms. Despite PLF’s technical potential, adoption across the livestock sector remains uneven, and stakeholder perceptions of these technologies vary widely. This study provides a meta-analysis of empirical research examining adoption, acceptance, and stakeholder perceptions of PLF technologies, aiming to identify key social determinants shaping the diffusion of digital livestock technologies. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a registered protocol (PROSPERO: CRD420261282807), systematic literature searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed/MEDLINE. Twenty-nine peer-reviewed studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the quantitative synthesis, contributing 421 study-level effect-size estimates that constituted the unit of analysis. Random-effects meta-analysis (restricted maximum likelihood, REML) was used to estimate pooled adoption rates, acceptance scores, and perception outcomes across stakeholder groups, with heterogeneity assessed using I2 statistics, and within-study dependence addressed through cluster-robust variance estimation (RVE, CR2). As approximate summary patterns rather than firm benchmarks given the still-limited evidence base — the pooled estimate indicates that adoption of any PLF technology pooled to approximately 53% (95% CI: 38–68%; five studies), whereas adoption of individual technologies pooled to only ∼17% (95% CI: 12–22%; 146 estimates from 16 studies) — most stakeholders use at least one PLF tool, but uptake of specific technologies remains low. In this study, acceptance refers to stakeholder attitudes or evaluations of PLF technologies measured on Likert-type scales (additionally rescaled to a percent-of-maximum-possible (POMP, 0–100) metric to enable cross-scale comparability), while perception refers to the direction and valence of stakeholder views, including the proportion expressing positive assessments. Perception analyses suggest that approximately 69.0% (95% CI: 63.5–74.0%; k = 69 effect sizes from 7 studies) of respondents expressed positive views of PLF technologies, and pooled acceptance and perception scores on the POMP metric were approximately 71.5% (95% CI: 68.2–74.8%) and 63.2% (95% CI: 59.1–67.3%), respectively. However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across all outcome categories (I 2 > 90%), and all pooled estimates should be interpreted with appropriate caution as indicative patterns rather than precise benchmarks. A principal methodological limitation of this synthesis is the very high between-study heterogeneity and the small number of eligible studies (k = 29; 421 effect-size estimates clustered within studies). The results suggest a gap between positive stakeholder attitudes and actual technology uptake. These findings highlight the importance of addressing economic, technical, and institutional barriers to facilitate broader adoption of PLF technologies and support socially responsive digital transformation in livestock systems. To the best of our knowledge, this synthesis provides the first quantitative estimates of PLF adoption and perception rates across stakeholder groups and livestock sectors, though the small evidence base warrants cautious interpretation. The findings offer actionable insights for policymakers, technology developers, and agricultural advisors seeking to align digital livestock innovations with stakeholder needs, institutional capacities, and societal expectations for responsible agricultural transformation.

Trajectory-synchronized diode laser actuation and dose-response field evaluation for precision weed control using a delta robot
abstract: Weed control in Vidalia onion production is constrained by a narrow management window, where delays in intervention can result in yield losses of up to 96% in direct-seeded systems. This challenge often forces growers to rely on costly transplanting practices and labor-intensive hand weeding, while the limited availability of effective post-emergence herbicides further restricts in-season control options. Robotic laser weeding offers a precise, non-chemical alternative by selectively targeting individual weeds while protecting crop health and minimizing environmental impact. This research introduces the application of a delta parallel robot equipped with a 60 W diode laser to achieve photothermal weed control by targeting the leaf emergence point (LEP). The manipulator used a lightweight structure, combining aluminum proximal arms with carbon fiber distal arms to support fast motion with limited vibration. A microcontroller-based control stack executed analytical inverse kinematics and synchronized waypoint sequencing, with transistor-transistor logic (TTL) based laser triggering to ensure precise synchronization between motion and laser actuation. The motion planner excluded targets outside the robot workspace and adaptively reduced speed in regions approaching kinematic singularities to maintain stability and accuracy. Positional accuracy was evaluated in a greenhouse setting across 100 commanded targets, yielding a mean radial error of 0.83 mm. Moreover, field positional validation across five sites yielded a mean radial error of 1.11 mm and a 95 th percentile error of 1.50 mm. Field experiments were conducted using Brassica rapa ‘Twister’, selected for its uniform morphology (canopy width: 10.0 ± 1.5 cm, height: 5.0 ± 1.5 cm), arranged in a completely randomized design. Treatments consisted of laser exposure durations of 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 s at 60 W, with 10 replicates per treatment level. Weed injury was quantified using Chlorophyll Content Index (CCI), visual necrosis, half rosette span, and plant height. Measurements were collected prior to treatment and at 0 (control), 24, 36, 48 and 240 h (10 d) post-treatment. By 10 days after treatment, CCI decreased by 92% and 59% at exposure durations of 3 s and 2 s, respectively. Correspondingly, weed mortality reached 90% at 3 s and 60% at 2 s. In contrast, 1 s and 0.5 s exposures induced only transient injury, followed by recovery, with no mortality observed in controls. Overall, the system delivered repeatable millimeter-scale dosing with deterministic motion-actuation synchronization. Integrating perception and navigation modules could further extend this framework toward fully automated, non-chemical weed control in Vidalia onion production systems.

A conditional scenario-analysis tool for base feed selection in precision-fed pig: Balancing feed cost and nitrogen excretion
abstract: The strategic formulation of base feeds in precision feeding (PF) systems for growing-finishing pigs remains a critical upstream challenge for balancing production costs and nitrogen (N) excretion. This study evaluated a conditional scenario-analysis tool designed to identify optimal standardized ileal digestible lysine (SID Lys) concentrations for high-protein (H) and low-protein (L) base feeds. Daily feed intake and body weight records from 179 Duroc × (Large White × Landrace) barrows (days 17 to 84 of fattening) were used as a fixed performance baseline. A simulation pipeline explored a grid of 1,368H/L feed combinations (H: 10.1–11.8 g/kg SID Lys; L: 2.5–10.0 g/kg SID Lys) across three historical feed price scenarios (September 2021, July 2022, and March 2023). Feasible candidate feeds were filtered using a dual feasibility criterion based on the i100 limitation index (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test P ≥ 0.05 and median i100 difference ≤ 1.5 percentage points relative to the trial). Formulations with H feed below 11.5 g/kg SID Lys systematically increased nutrient inadequacy (P < 0.05). Retained candidate pairs demonstrated that H = 11.5 g/kg SID Lys achieved minimal feed cost per animal across all price scenarios, while optimal L feed concentrations shifted between 6.6, 7.9, and 7.6 g/kg SID Lys depending on ingredient market volatility. From an environmental perspective, H = 11.5 g/kg and L = 7.4 g/kg SID Lys minimized estimated N excretion to 43.34% of N intake (1.245 kg N/animal). Temporal clustering of the fattening period into three phases yielded only marginal feed cost reductions compared to a single full-period base feed specification. Consequently, swine operations can prioritize a single, robust pair of base feeds (11.5 g/kg H and intermediate L) managed via daily dynamic blending without increasing operational or logistical complexity.

Field portable soil spectroscopy: What’s beyond Vis-NIR?
abstract: The use of spectroscopy in soil properties measurement has been extensively investigated. To qualify and quantify soils with high speed and accuracy, field portable soil spectroscopy (FPSS) is a promising tool to carry out in situ soil surveys. These sensors can produce continuous spectra from different chemical principles, and soil properties can be either directly or indirectly inferred from the spectra. This review summarised the theories and applications of eight FPSS, including some already widely implemented and some still in an early stage of development. These FPSS are characterised by the information they provide, namely organic, mineralogical, elemental, and physical information about soils. Visible, near-infrared and mid-infrared spectroscopy methods are the primary vibrational spectroscopy method used to measure organic and mineralogical properties. Raman spectroscopy, another vibrational spectroscopy, is also promising, but requires more quantitative validation. X-ray fluorescence and laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy are effective in quantifying elemental concentrations and are commonly used as complementary sensors to the vibrational spectroscopy. Gamma-ray spectroscopy detects gamma radiation and is used to identify and quantify radioactive elements. Lastly, nuclear magnetic resonance and terahertz spectroscopy are two emerging sensors that have the potential to characterise organic matter and soil physical properties, respectively.

Precision livestock farming and farm animal welfare: a scientometric analysis of research trends and technological innovations
abstract: Precision Livestock Farming (PLF) is increasingly recognized for its potential to improve the health and welfare of farm animals, their productivity, and environmental sustainability. Nevertheless, the critical transition of PLF from a theoretical research concept to practical field implementation remains essential for realizing its full potential. This study undertakes a scientometric review of PLF and its application in the monitoring of farm animal welfare, covering the period from 2006 to 2025. The study employs a mixed-corpus scientometric approach to concurrently assess trends in PLF publications (n = 1,594) and patents (n = 3,239), revealing a strong co-evolutionary relationship (r = 0.913, 95% CI 0.79–0.97, p < 0.001) between academic and industrial PLF activity, with annual growth rates of 32.2% and 20.2%, respectively. The analysis identifies key research subfields and traces the evolution of PLF themes across three overlapping phases: a hardware validation phase (2006–2015), a welfare outcome validation phase (2016–2020), and an artificial intelligence integration phase (2021–2025). The study underscores the importance of integrating scientific literature and patent data for comprehensive insights into PLF’s role in enhancing farm animal welfare and highlights persistent gaps between proof-of-concept research and commercially deployed, welfare-validated systems.

Weather-based prediction of black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia L.) honey yield and quality: a reproducible computational system with operational deployment
abstract: Black locust (Robinia pseudoacacia L.; marketed as “acacia”) honey production in South Korea—accounting for over 70% of national honey output—has been increasingly affected by weather-driven disturbances, resulting in substantial production declines, notably in 2018 and 2020 ( Kim et al., 2022 ). Such episodes have been broadly attributed to impacts of climate change; however, a diagnostic framework identifying which weather variables, and at which phenological stages, drive the simultaneous decline in yield and quality has remained unavailable. Existing approaches rely either on uninterpretable machine-learning models that require large training data unavailable at the farm scale, or on single-variable rules-of-thumb that fail under multivariate weather conditions. Therefore, we present a reproducible computational system that addresses this gap through three integrated components: (i) two interpretable hierarchical weather indices—the Honey Harvest Weather Index (HHWI) for yield and the Honey Moisture Weather Index (HMWI) for moisture content—derived from five meteorological variables (maximum temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation) across three phenological stages (bud formation, pre-flowering, and flowering); (ii) a generalized raster pipeline producing spatially-explicit predictions from gridded meteorological data; (iii) an operational forecast module generating real-time decision-support maps via inverse-distance interpolation. The system was validated using 570 farm-year records from 95 black locust apiaries (2020–2025) in South Korea and benchmarked against seven machine-learning alternatives. HHWI achieved a cross-validated R2 value of 0.395 (RMSE = 16.85 kg/colony) using three effective parameters and outperformed XGBoost in terms of cross-validated stability, exhibiting a 15-fold reduction in the overfitting gap. HMWI achieved a cross-validated R2 value of 0.668, with a moisture-grade classification accuracy of 96.0% (within ± 1 grade, Cohen’s κ = 0.41). This demonstrates its operational feasibility for weather-based quality prediction. Retrospective decomposition of the 2020 production minimum (18.4 kg/colony) indicated that approximately 60% of the deficit relative to the 2024 peak year (60.5 kg/colony) was attributable to maximum temperature during the pre-flowering stage. Cumulative temperature contributions across all phenological stages accounted for 80% of the deficit, transforming broad climate-change attribution into actionable diagnoses of specific weather variables and phenological stages. The data-driven breakpoints converged with published physiological thresholds for Apis mellifera , supporting the mechanistic interpretation. The complete system—including analysis script, raster pipeline, forecast module, and 22-checkpoint verification—was released as an open-source code, providing beekeepers and policymakers with a deployment-ready, weather-based decision-support system that requires only routine meteorological data. All codes and anonymized data are available on Zenodo ( https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20612458) .

From visible to yield-contributing opened bolls: An interpretable PAI-based correction framework for cotton boll estimation under canopy occlusion in UAV imagery
abstract: Accurate estimation of yield-contributing opened cotton boll density from UAV imagery is limited by canopy occlusion, because nadir-view detection models can only identify opened bolls exposed on the canopy surface. To address this problem, this study developed an interpretable correction framework that converts visible opened boll density into yield-contributing opened boll density by incorporating Plant Area Index (PAI) as a canopy-structure proxy. The framework integrates a position-specific lightweight YOLOv8n detector, a sliding-window and deduplication-based plot-scale counting pipeline, and a PAI-based correction model. Field data collected from 2023 to 2025 were used, with the 2024 dataset serving for detector training, counting-pipeline development, and correction-model calibration, while the 2023 and 2025 datasets were reserved for independent cross-year validation. The improved detector achieved an mAP@0.50:0.95 of 0.789, with 2.15 million parameters and an inference time of 2.90 ms. In the 2024 calibration dataset, the PAI-integrated correction model reduced the estimation error from 8.26% using visible opened boll density alone to 3.48%, with an RMSE of 5.09 bolls·m −2 . In independent validation across 102 plots from 2023 and 2025, the framework achieved an overall MAPE of 2.24%, with treatment-level errors ranging from 0.20% to 8.58%. The resolution sensitivity analysis indicated that the framework remained stable when the spatial resolution was finer than 0.37 cm·pixel −1 . These results demonstrate that explicitly modeling canopy occlusion with PAI enables a robust and interpretable conversion from visible opened boll counts to yield-contributing opened boll density estimates, providing a practical pathway for UAV-based organ-scale cotton phenotyping and yield-component assessment.

Lightweight real-time detection of sweet potato virus disease by a hybrid CNN–Transformer network
abstract: Timely and precise detection of sweet potato virus disease (SPVD) is essential for ensuring crop health and improving yield quality in precision agriculture. However, conventional deep learning models often struggle to capture subtle lesion features under complex field conditions. This paper proposes Swin-SPVDNet, a hybrid CNN-Transformer detection framework with task-specific architectural enhancements that combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with a modified Swin Transformer to effectively integrate local spatial details and global contextual information. Unlike conventional hybrid models that simply stack convolutional and transformer blocks, the proposed network introduces three key structural designs: (1) A C2PSA-enhanced convolutional backbone for improved local feature sensitivity. (2) A C3STR module that tightly integrates convolutional operations with Swin Transformer blocks for joint local–global feature interaction. (3) A Residual Attention Block (RAB) that refines feature representations while stabilizing gradient propagation. A field-collected SPVD image dataset was constructed using handheld RGB imaging under real agricultural conditions. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that Swin-SPVDNet achieves competitive performance compared with representative state-of-the-art detectors while providing a favorable balance between detection accuracy and deployment efficiency, attaining a mean Average Precision (mAP@0.5) of 86.8%, a precision of 85.1%, and a recall of 75.6%. Compared to Yolov5-v11 models, our approach demonstrates improved robustness in detecting small and irregular lesions, particularly under occlusion and lighting variability. These results confirm the practical value of Swin-SPVDNet for real-time field deployment and support its application in intelligent disease monitoring.

Adapting SAM3 for 3D fruit counting with cross-view contrastive learning and Hough voting
abstract: Fruit detection and 3D localization have been shown to be critical for precision agriculture applications, such as yield estimation and robot harvesting tasks. However, real-world agricultural settings can be associated with high density of fruits, strong occlusions, and variable illumination, leading to difficulty in accurately detecting and localizing fruits. Although there exist 2D approaches dedicated for fruit counting, these approaches may easily merge adjacent fruits due to projection effects in dense occlusions, thus limiting their effectiveness. Motivated by this, in this paper, we explore the problem of 3D fruit detection and localization with vision foundation model adaptation and 3D Gaussian-based scene representation. Particularly, we use low-rank adaptation to leverage SAM3 to generate high-quality instance masks with different crops and illuminations. Meanwhile, to address noisy pseudo label issue, we adopt cross-view contrastive learning with uncertainty weighting for enhanced 3D feature representation. Moreover, we devise a Hough voting procedure in the 3D Gaussian space to integrate multi-view evidence of occluded fruits, followed by clustering to estimate the number of fruits as well as their 3D locations. The proposed approach has been extensively tested with thousands of fruits from synthetic orchard scenes, real apple orchard datasets, as well as greenhouse sweet pepper scenes. Experiment results show significant performance gains for densely occluded cases, with the F1-scores reaching 0.971 and 0.977 for plum and mango, respectively. Meanwhile, our approach can achieve more than a twofold boost for 3D instance segmentation over FruitNeRF. More notably, the adapted weights and the post-processing settings transfer from the open-field apple orchard to greenhouse sweet pepper scenes, where only the SAM3 text prompt is changed and the 3D Gaussian representation is still optimized for each new scene.

Coupling modeling, design optimization, and experimental research of agrivoltaic systems based on soybean cultivation
abstract: As an effective approach to mitigate land competition between energy and agricultural production, agrivoltaic systems face the core challenge of balancing light demands for photovoltaic power generation and crop growth. In this paper, taking the agrivoltaic system for soybean cultivation as the research object, an optimized design method that integrates multiple sub-models and multi-objective optimization is proposed. A coupled model that includes ground irradiance model, photovoltaic power generation model, and soybean yield model is constructed, and the Kriging model combined with the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) is applied to conduct multi-objective optimization on photovoltaic tilt angle, mounting height, and row spacing, obtaining a Pareto optimal solution set. A soybean planting experiment lasting over three months verifies the model’s reliability. The results show a trade-off between power generation and soybean yield. During the soybean growing season,the power generation corresponding to the Pareto optimal solution ranges from 364,635 to 364,639 kWh, and the soybean yield ranges from 2,800 to 3,200 kg/ha. The photovoltaic tilt angle (peak at 45°) dominates power generation, row spacing is most critical for yield, and mounting height interacts with the other two parameters. The proposed model and method provide quantitative support for the design of agrivoltaic systems tailored to different regions and objectives.

title: Vision-guided robotic harvesting of Toona sinensis sprouts: Integrating biomechanical calibration with improved YOLO instance segmentation
From sky to ground: Enabling autonomous vineyard traversal with UAV-derived navigation maps
abstract: Reliable structural maps are essential for deploying autonomous ground robots in vineyards, yet producing these maps often still depends on manual real-time kinematic (RTK) surveying or teleoperated data collection. This bottleneck slows robotic deployment and can limit the reuse of spatial data within broader digital-vineyard workflows. In this paper, we present an operational aerial-to-ground pipeline that converts overlapping nadir Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery into robot-ready vineyard maps. The pipeline integrates structural detection, metadata-driven geospatial projection, spatial clustering, and occupancy/topological map generation. By extracting features directly from raw overlapping frames, the system bypasses computationally expensive orthomosaic processing, accelerating the map generation timeline. We evaluate robustness across multiple seasons and flight altitudes, reporting map-level performance and robotic deployment feasibility. Using August 39 ft imagery, all five evaluated models produced sub-metre maps; YOLO11 segmentation achieved an RMSE of 0.242 m, while YOLO11 object detection reached a perfect map-level F1-score. A supplementary best-case capability analysis identified a minimum RMSE of 0.207 m using YOLO11 segmentation on March 39 ft imagery. Field trials on a Thorvald robotic platform, over approximately 500 m of autonomous row traversal per generated map, demonstrated reliable navigation, achieving a Mean Distance Between Interventions (MDBI) of up to 161.4 m. Furthermore, UAV data collection was consistently faster than baseline methods, cutting field survey time by up to 94% compared to robotic teleoperation in a 2.4-hectare commercial-vineyard scalability study. These results demonstrate that overlapping UAV imagery provides a practical route to generating vineyard navigation maps that support autonomous deployment under the tested conditions.

Video-based fruit detection and tracking: effects of scanning conditions on fruit load estimation
abstract: Automated fruit counting and yield estimation systems are necessary for efficient orchard management. This study presents a computer vision system based on video multi-object-tracking for fruit load estimation in apple orchards and provides a comprehensive analysis of the system performance under diverse scanning conditions. The system integrates fruit detection, tracking, localization within orchard, and fruit load map generation. Experiments were carried out in an experimental apple orchard containing 420 apple trees. Data was collected with two different RGB-D sensors (Azure Kinect DK and ZED 2) at three different scanning distances (125 cm, 175 cm, and 225 cm) on two different dates prior to the harvest. Comparing the two evaluated sensors, Azure Kinect provided more consistent performance across different dates. Results also show that the longer scanning distance improves accuracy due to seeing the full tree view gives better fruit counts than close partial views. Between the two dates, best results were achieved near harvest due to fruit color at this stage, achieving a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 6.91 % and a determination coefficient (R 2 ) of 0.733 (using ZED2 sensor at 225 cm distance). Finally, a test comparing scanning from one or both sides of the tree row showed that bilateral scanning improved fruit load estimation at the stretch level by incorporating information from both sides of the canopy. The results of this work demonstrate the effectiveness of the video fruit tracking systems as a useful tool for automating fruit load estimation.

title: FlowDelayNet: self-supervised siamese learning for automated flow-delay estimation in yield monitor data
abstract: Yield monitor data are widely used for management zone delineation, prescription map development, and on-farm decision making; however, delay in the data caused by sensor response latency can misassign yield measurements to incorrect locations. Existing correction methods often rely on manual tuning, or handcrafted similarity measures that are sensitive to noise, missing data, and irregular harvesting geometry. This study proposes FlowDelayNet, a self-supervised deep learning framework for estimating field-level flow delay by learning delay-aware spatial representations. FlowDelayNet employs a Siamese convolutional encoder trained to discriminate whether two yield patches have similar or dissimilar delays. A dataset of 632 harvested fields was split at the field level into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%). Yield surfaces were rasterized over candidate delays from −15 to +15 logging intervals, and overlapping patches (24 × 24, stride 12) were extracted. A Gaussian-based spatial smoothness score computed using correlation analysis provided the self-supervised supervisory signal. Model optimization combined contrastive loss on Siamese embeddings with regression loss against the normalized smoothness signal. Compared to hard-argmax selection, a temperature-scaled soft-argmax formulation improves delay estimation by computing the expected delay. Across 95 fields, the mean absolute error was 1.24 delay units, with 64 fields predicted within ±1 delay relative to the Gaussian spatial smoothness reference. Embedding analysis showed a mean anchor–positive distance of 0.25 compared to 0.72 for anchor–negative pairs, with 94.8% of sampled triplets satisfying AP < AN. These results demonstrate that FlowDelayNet provides an automated and robust solution for flow-delay estimation across heterogeneous field conditions.

title: Semantic risk-aware motion planning for apple young-fruit thinning manipulators
abstract: Thinning young apple fruits is a key practice for regulating tree load and improving fruit quality, yet manual thinning is labour-intensive and constrained by narrow operational windows. To address the challenges of dense fruit clusters and the coexistence of rigid and flexible obstacles, this study proposes a Semantic Risk-Aware RRT* (SRA-RRT*) algorithm for autonomous robotic thinning. The method employs YOLOv11-seg for instance segmentation of fruit clusters, using anchor box centres as end-effector targets. A dual-layer risk field is constructed, with rigid structures as hard constraints and flexible canopy elements assigned semantic risk values to enable low-risk traversal. Risk-guided sampling and bidirectional adaptive tree expansion improve search efficiency, and Catmull-Rom splines smooth paths to generate continuous, executable end-effector motion.Simulation results indicate that in four types of 2D grid environments, SRA-RRT* achieves an average planning time of 0.15-0.54 s with 100% success. In two 3D orchard scenarios, average planning times are 0.41 s and 0.64 s, with path lengths of 173.97 m and 173.12 m, both with 100% success. Compared with RRT*, FMT*, BIT*, AIT*, APF-RRT*, and RRT-Connect, planning times are reduced by 24.7-95.1% and path lengths by 1.6-17.1%. Single-cluster continuous thinning simulations achieve 93.33% success, while physical experiments confirm reductions of 18.8-97.0% in planning time, 12.1-20.4% in path length, a planning success rate of 91.67%, and a single-cluster operation time of 28.4 s.These results demonstrate that SRA-RRT* provides a safe, efficient, and smooth motion planning solution for autonomous thinning of young apple fruits.

Thermal performance of a passive solar heating system for tropical greenhouse heating: Experimental and CFD analysis
abstract: Thermal inversion is a common problem in tropical highland greenhouses, where nocturnal radiative cooling promotes cold air accumulation near the crop canopy and reduces microclimatic stability. This study experimentally and numerically evaluated the thermal performance of a passive solar heating system for nocturnal greenhouse heating under tropical conditions. The system consisted of a solar thermal collector, a photovoltaic-powered recirculation pump, and a radiant floor heating pipe. Experimental measurements, energy balance analysis, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, and a techno-economic assessment were conducted to investigate heat-transfer behavior, airflow patterns, and economic feasibility. The passive heating system increased the greenhouse air temperature by 1.11 ± 0.18 °C relative to outdoor conditions and maintained a stable vertical thermal gradient that mitigated nocturnal thermal inversion. Energy balance analysis showed that the heating pipe supplied 69.6% of the total thermal input, whereas the roof accounted for approximately 66% of total thermal losses. The validated CFD model accurately reproduced the experimental thermal behavior (MAE = 0.187 °C) and revealed a buoyancy-driven bicellular airflow pattern associated with vertical thermal stratification inside the greenhouse. The economic analysis demonstrated a competitive levelized cost of energy of 0.15 USD kWh−1 and a positive net present value of 578.65 USD over a 20-year period. Overall, the proposed system represents a technically reliable and economically viable strategy for improving nocturnal greenhouse microclimates under tropical conditions.

ArchiCrop: Crop model dynamics downscaled to 3D+t plant architecture
abstract: Abstract Evolving agricultural practices and contexts invite to reconsider the way crop and plant models represent agroecosystem processes. Crop models assume spatial homogeneity, which reduces confidence in their predictions for structurally heterogeneous systems, whereas FSPMs’ complexity limits their application to field-scale or large-scale studies. To benefit from strengths of both approaches, we introduce ArchiCrop, a parametric 3D architectural model of cereals that generates plant geometries constrained by crop model dynamics and coordination rules. Inspired by the concept of equifinality, ArchiCrop generates a morphospace of architecturally diverse morphotypes which remain equivalent at crop scale in terms of LAI and height. This multiscale approach enables the comparison of processes computed at different scales on wheat, rice, maize and sorghum. We demonstrate its application evaluating light interception Beer’s formalism in STICS soil-crop model relying on the leaf-resolved radiosity model Caribu for the 3D reference simulations, for a sorghum monocrop. We show that the consideration of the variability of only two plant architectural traits, leaf insertion angle and leaf number, introduces up to 27% of uncertainty in the cumulated absorbed light at the end of the season. A possible outcome from this method is also the definition of metamodels for crop model processes, as exemplified for extinction coefficient of Beer’s law. ArchiCrop can support a range of applications, including crop model uncertainty analysis, model-assisted phenotyping, and ideotype design. Highlights ArchiCrop is the first 3D+t botany-based parametric generative model for cereals. ArchiCrop downscales crop model dynamics to 3D+t architecture canopies efficiently. ArchiCrop compares big leaf versus leaf-resolved light interception. Plant architectures with same leaf area intercept light with up to 27% variability. ArchiCrop helps ideotyping, crop model evaluation and error propagation analysis. Graphical abstract

Design and evaluation of a hybrid fin-ray finger with inflatable soft pads for apple harvesting under leaf interference
abstract: This paper presents the design, modelling, and experimental validation of a Hybrid Fin-Ray Finger (HFRF) integrating segmented inflatable Dragon Skin 30 silicone membrane pads for adaptive and bruise-free robotic apple harvesting. Harvesting fruits within cluttered canopy environments demands a balance between gentle contact to prevent bruising and sufficient pulling and detachment torque. However, conventional Fin-Ray fingers often exhibit limited torsional resistance, non-uniform force distribution, and reduced contact area, leading to slip and localized pressure concentrations on the fruit surface. To overcome these limitations, we integrate inflatable soft membrane pads into the Fin-Ray structure, increasing the effective finger width and improving surface conformity and pressure distribution. An analytical model is developed to predict membrane deformation and contact angle as a function of internal pressure, and the results are validated through finite element simulations and experimental testing. Pressure-sensitive film experiments demonstrate that Dragon Skin 30 inflation at 30 kPa increased contact area by up to 40% and reduced mean contact pressure by 11% relative to the unpressurised configuration, while EcoFlex 00–30 exhibited volumetric expansion under pressure that reduced conformal contact across the tested range. Performance evaluations were conducted under three standardized leaf interference conditions (0%, 50%, and 100% occlusion) using real Pink Lady apple leaves, with statistical analysis performed using one-way ANOVA and Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons. At 30 kPa without leaf interference, normal detachment force increased by 148% relative to the no-pad configuration and torsional moment increased by 58% relative to the unpressurised condition, while maintaining performance above the detachment threshold. Under full leaf occlusion, torsional performance collapsed regardless of inflation pressure, identifying full canopy occlusion as the primary limiting factor for torsional resistance. These results confirm that the proposed HFRF provides pressure-adaptive, slip-resistant, and bruise-mitigating grasping performance suitable for robotic apple harvesting in unstructured orchard environments.

title: Use of smartphone images in the evaluation of weed control with glyphosate: A computational approach using Random Forest
abstract: The evaluation of herbicide control efficacy is essential in integrated weed management, and this information is fed back into the database for future crop protection actions. The evaluation of weed control using herbicides is carried out based on on-site visual evaluations, which can be time-consuming and imprecise. In this study, models capable of evaluating the efficacy of Urochloa brizantha control by glyphosate were proposed using computational image analysis with Random Forest. The images were obtained with a smartphone in an area with U. brizantha infestation desiccated by glyphosate. To stratify the control response, glyphosate doses of 0, 144, 288, 576, 864, 1152, and 1440 g a.e. ha −1 were applied. For model estimation, 27 vegetation indices were used as input variables, with the objective of estimating control based on visual evaluation data and on control percentage data determined by the plant mass killed by the action of the herbicide. The model developed with data from visual control scores presented excellent performance, both in training (r 2 of 0.92) and in validation (r 2 of 0.92). The model trained with the percentage of dead plant mass also presented satisfactory performance, with an r 2 of 0.88 for the training sample and 0.90 for the validation sample. The proposed evaluation method presents advantages over the usual methods, due to the ease of obtaining smartphone images and the possibility of inserting the indices and models developed in mobile applications.

StomataSeg: Semi-supervised instance segmentation for sorghum stomatal components
abstract: Sorghum is a globally important cereal grown widely in water-limited and stress-prone regions. Its strong drought tolerance makes it a priority crop for climate-resilient agriculture. Improving water-use efficiency in sorghum requires precise characterization of stomatal traits, as stomata control of gas exchange, transpiration and photosynthesis have a major influence on crop performance. Automated analysis of sorghum stomata is difficult because the stomata are small (often less than 40 μ m in length in grasses such as sorghum) and vary in shape across genotypes and leaf surfaces. Automated segmentation contributes to high-throughput stomatal phenotyping, yet current methods still face challenges related to nested small structures and annotation bottlenecks. In this paper, we propose a unified semi-supervised instance segmentation framework for multi-class segmentation of three nested sorghum stomatal components. We collect and annotate a sorghum leaf imagery dataset containing 11,060 human-annotated patches, covering the three stomatal components (pore, guard cell and complex area) across multiple genotypes and leaf surfaces. To improve the detection of tiny structures, we split high-resolution microscopy images into overlapping small patches. We then apply a pseudo-labelling strategy with class-specific confidence filtering and expert verification to unannotated images, producing an additional 56,428 pseudo-labelled patches. Patch-based preprocessing increases the top semantic segmentation mIoU from 65.93% to 70.35% and the top instance segmentation AP from 28.30% to 46.10%. Subsequent pseudo-label retraining further increases overall AP from 46.10% to 49.20% for Mask R-CNN with ConvNeXt-V2. These results demonstrate that combining patch-based preprocessing with semi-supervised learning significantly improves the segmentation of fine stomatal structures. The proposed framework supports scalable extraction of stomatal traits and facilitates broader adoption of AI-driven phenotyping in crop science.

title: Agri-CPJ: A training-free explainable framework for agricultural pest diagnosis using Caption-Prompt-Judge and LLM-as-a-Judge
Improved point cloud segmentation algorithms for in situ individual plant phenotyping and weight prediction of Chinese cabbage plants using UAV imagery
abstract: With the advancement of precision agriculture and modern breeding techniques, large-scale, efficient, and in situ acquisition of plant phenotypic data has become a critical challenge in research. Traditional manual measurement methods are inefficient and struggle to meet the demand for high-throughput phenotypic data in modern breeding. Consequently, this study proposes a method based on low-altitude drones and three-dimensional (3D) point cloud analysis to achieve in situ, nondestructive phenotypic extraction and weight prediction for individual Chinese cabbage plants. First, RGB images are captured in the field using unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Large-scale 3D point clouds are reconstructed through structure from motion with multiview stereo technology. Subsequently, an enhanced graph convolutional neural network (AW-GNN) is proposed, integrating wavelet convolution, adaptive graph structure learning, and attention mechanisms to improve the accuracy and robustness of point cloud semantic segmentation. Building on this foundation, a morphology-guided watershed clustering algorithm is introduced. High-density segmentation of individual plants can be achieved in crowded environments by integrating two-dimensional canopy height maps with 3D point cloud spatial information. Based on the segmentation results, 3D phenotypic parameters, such as plant height, canopy width, and volume, are extracted. Individual plant weight prediction models are constructed using machine learning methods, including support vector regression (SVR) and random forest. Experimental results demonstrate that AW-GNN achieves an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 91.63% in point cloud semantic segmentation, significantly outperforming existing mainstream models. Morphological watershed clustering effectively mitigates undersegmentation and oversegmentation problems encountered by traditional methods under dense plant conditions. For individual plant weight prediction, the SVR model delivers optimal performance with a validation set R 2 of 0.8691 and root mean square error of 0.2810 kg. This study demonstrates the feasibility of achieving individual plant phenotyping and weight prediction in large-scale in situ scenarios using a UAV platform and improved point cloud segmentation algorithms, thereby providing an effective technical approach for high-throughput plant phenotyping analysis and digital breeding decision-making.

A physics-informed, behavior-aware digital twin for robust multimodal forecasting of core body temperature in precision livestock farming
abstract: Precision livestock farming requires accurate and timely heat stress prediction to ensure animal welfare and optimize farm management. This study presents a physics-informed digital twin (DT) framework combined with an uncertainty-aware, expert-weighted stacked ensemble for multimodal forecasting of Core Body Temperature (CBT) in dairy cattle. Using the high-frequency, heterogeneous MmCows dataset, the DT integrates an ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based thermoregulation model that simulates metabolic heat production and dissipation, a Gaussian process for capturing cow-specific deviations, a Kalman filter for aligning predictions with real-time sensor data, and a behavioral Markov chain that models activity-state transitions under varying environmental conditions. The DT outputs key physiological indicators, such as predicted CBT, heat stress probability, and behavioral state distributions are fused with raw sensor data and enriched through multi-scale temporal analysis and cross-modal feature engineering to form a comprehensive feature set. The predictive methodology is designed in a three-stage stacked ensemble, where stage 1 trains modality-specific LightGBM ‘expert’ models on distinct feature groups, stage 2 collects their predictions as meta-features, and at stage 3 Optuna-tuned LightGBM meta-model yields the final CBT forecast. Predictive uncertainty is quantified via bootstrapping and validated using Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP). Ablation analysis confirms that incorporating DT-derived features and multimodal fusion substantially enhances performance. The proposed framework achieves a cross-validated R 2 of 0.783, F1 score of 84.25% and PICP of 92.38% for 2-hour ahead forecasting, providing a robust, uncertainty-aware, and physically principled system for early heat stress detection and precision livestock management.

Improving greenhouse fruit-production control by integrating reinforcement learning into short-horizon model predictive control
abstract: Greenhouse fruit-production control aims to maximize the economic performance (fruit revenue minus operating costs) while operating within system constraints under external weather disturbances. Control methods need to balance the delayed economic benefit of fruit yield with current operating costs. For such problems, model predictive control (MPC) can handle constraints under future weather disturbances, but can become computationally demanding when using sufficiently long prediction horizons for (relatively large) nonlinear greenhouse fruit production models. In contrast, reinforcement learning (RL) can learn control policies before deployment while considering economic performance beyond MPC’s prediction horizon. However, desired indoor climate ranges are typically incorporated through penalty terms, and performance may degrade under unseen weather trajectories. This work proposes trajectory-selection RL–MPC , a framework that incorporates the economic benefit of fruit yield beyond the MPC prediction horizon into a finite-horizon optimization problem with a relatively short horizon (one hour). The framework uses an RL rollout trajectory to define a terminal region constraint and terminal cost. Next, a nonlinear MPC solves a short-horizon optimization problem with these terminal ingredients to find a local optimum. Finally, the framework selects and executes the first input from the trajectory with the better objective value, either from the MPC-predicted or the RL rollout trajectory. The method is applied to GreenLight, a large-scale nonlinear greenhouse tomato production model that exhibits stiff dynamics. The simulation results show that trajectory-selection RL–MPC with a one-hour prediction horizon matches the closed-loop performance of a high-performing guiding policy while improving over standalone MPC with the same horizon. On 25 weather trajectories held out during policy training, trajectory-selection RL–MPC achieved ∼ 52 % higher closed-loop performance than standalone RL and ∼ 80 % higher performance than MPC with the same horizon length.

Physiology-guided multi-objective machine learning for robust fructose prediction in Asian pear under interannual climate variability
abstract: Predicting Asian pear fructose concentration under interannual climate variability is challenging because sugar accumulation reflects cumulative interactions among developmental progression, environmental conditions, and prior metabolic state. Using a six-year repeated-measures field dataset from ‘Niitaka’ Asian pear trees, fructose concentration at N days after full bloom (DAFB) was predicted from meteorological and phenological descriptors aligned to each DAFB sampling window and sugar measurements from the preceding sampling point (N − 15 DAFB). We developed a physiology-guided machine learning framework using XGBoost as a fixed regressor and three feature-transformation components: a climate gate that weights precursor-history signals by stage-specific environmental conditions, a Richards growth kernel that constrains developmental trajectories, and lagged sugar features that represent metabolic continuity. Representation parameters were optimized under six-fold leave-one-year-out cross-validation using scalarized single-objective optimization or nondominated sorting genetic algorithm III (NSGA-III), targeting the mean, maximum, and standard deviation of yearwise root mean square error (RMSE). The selected multi-objective model achieved a pooled RMSE of 35.48 mg·g −1 dry weight (DW), compared with 55.53 mg·g −1 DW for the climate–phenology baseline, reducing pooled error by 36.1% and interannual variability by 70.4%. Pareto front analysis revealed an accuracy–robustness trade-off and supported the selection of an operationally balanced solution for reliable fruit-quality prediction.

Vision-guided row-aligned spraying system for soybean seedlings using an improved YOLO11s-seg model
abstract: Accurate alignment between spray bands and crop rows is a key requirement for canopy-directed band spraying in soybean fields. This study developed a vision-guided row-aligned spraying system intended for the banded application of products for foliar disease management or foliar fertilizers to soybean canopies. The system integrates instance segmentation, crop-row extraction, and lateral row-following control. First, an EC-YOLO11s-seg instance segmentation model was constructed based on YOLO11s-seg. The C3K2_EMBC module, CAFM (Convolution and Attention Fusion Module) attention mechanism, Shape-IoU loss, and EMASlideLoss were introduced. These components improved the model’s ability to learn multi-scale soybean seedling features, complex boundaries, and hard-to-classify samples. Second, a crop-row extraction method was developed based on instance segmentation masks. This method combines Monte Carlo sampling, inverse perspective mapping, DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) clustering, and least-squares fitting. It enables stable estimation of the spatial position and direction of soybean crop rows. Finally, the vision recognition algorithm, closed-loop lateral adjustment mechanism, and band spraying device were integrated into an electric self-propelled boom sprayer. Field experiments using clean water were conducted to evaluate row-alignment accuracy. The results showed that EC-YOLO11s-seg achieved P m a s k , R m a s k , and m A P 50 m a s k values of 88.96 %, 89.72 %, and 92.61 %, respectively, on a self-built cross-year soybean seedling field dataset. These values were 5.42, 5.58, and 5.20 percentage points higher than those of the baseline YOLO11s-seg model. The average inference speed was 62.82 FPS, indicating good offline inference efficiency. For crop-row extraction, the mean relative distance error, mean relative endpoint error, and mean angle error were 3.69 %, 5.18 %, and 1.43°, respectively. The mean fitting accuracy for row angle reached 0.9065. These results demonstrate good row localization accuracy and directional consistency. Field row-aligned spraying tests showed that the system maintained good row-following performance at operating speeds of 2–5 km/h. The mean lateral deviation ranged from 8.93 to 23.75 mm. The proportion of samples with a lateral deviation less than 10 % of the row spacing remained above 85.0 %. At 2–4 km/h, this proportion was not lower than 92.5 %. These results indicate that the proposed system has good perception accuracy, row-alignment capability, and operational stability under complex field conditions. It can support banded row-aligned spraying and reduce off-row application of foliar liquids in soybean fields at the seedling stage.

title: Mango-SparseInst: A two-stage framework for instance segmentation and picking point localization in automated mango harvesting
Spatially-aware consensus-based bundling for event-triggered multi-harvester row allocation
abstract: Assigning crop rows to several harvesters requires accounting for row lengths, machine speeds, and changes during the mission. We present an event-triggered allocator that combines consensus-inspired bundling with nearest-row filtering, proximity admission, and speed-aware balancing that also works inside a fragmented radio network. On 100-row fields we compare executed allocations with a centralized fixed-sweep dynamic program, a static speed split, and textbook CBBA. With full connectivity the method is within 6.2% of the dynamic program, and its makespan is within 1% of textbook CBBA while it needs about 3 consensus rounds instead of 36 to 51 and keeps each machine on a contiguous block. After failures, joins, and speed changes, frozen plans leave up to 20% of rows unharvested, whereas the method completes every row. With only local information, heartbeat failure detection, and a 50 m radio range, it recovers no more than 2.2% slower than a base-station coordinator and within 6% of an oracle with global state, without needing the base station. Packet loss of up to 30% changes its completion time by less than 1%, and 1 s of latency per hop by at most 2.3%. Straight-line deadhead is 2.6% to 3.1% of travel, and a 30 m turn allowance per row transition raises nonproductive travel to 14.8%. The results come from simulation with simplified vehicle motion; field validation remains future work.

title: Gas characterization pattern-guided adaptive modeling algorithm: Method and mechanism for non-destructive detection of silage quality using a colorimetric sensor array

Hyperspectral olive maturity estimation model for table olives: A non-invasive proof-of-concept study
abstract: The economic significance of olive cultivation and trade is paramount for Mediterranean countries, yielding a substantial impact on their respective local economies. However, the quality of olives is significantly influenced by the harvest timing, which occurs when they reach optimal size and maturity stage. Conventionally, farmers have relied on empirical observation to determine the optimal harvest date, guided by their accumulated expertise and knowledge. While this approach is well-founded, it lacks the rigor and objectivity offered by data-driven methods. The development of an automatic system for determining olive maturity is a significant concern for the industry. This study proposes an artificial intelligence-based system for estimating the maturity of table olives using a novel technological approach. The method involves the identification of olive maturity stages through field methods that utilize proximal hyperspectral imaging technology. A comprehensive analysis was conducted to elucidate the importance of each spectral band and to assess the model’s performance with a reduced feature space. In this proof-of-concept study, a Hyperspectral Olive Maturity Estimation Model (HOMEM) was developed to estimate olives’ maturity by determining their Maturity Index. The model employed visible and near-infrared spectral signatures acquired through in-field hyperspectral imaging. The present study explores the precision of HOMEM and the impact of normalization with hyperspectral images employing various AI-based models. The proposed HOMEM model attained an R2 value of 93 % in its estimation of the Maturity Index through the utilization of visible and near-infrared wavelengths. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of hyperspectral imaging and machine learning techniques to enhance the assessment of olive quality and reduce reliance on traditional, experience-based methods.

title: A low-stress and accurate method for dead chicken detection in commercial caged poultry houses without supplemental lighting
Research on the strawberry picking point localization algorithm based on dual-stage lightweight networks
Lightweight autonomous construction and application of a knowledge graph for soil acidification constraint management based on LLM agents
abstract: In the red and yellow soil regions of southern China, long-term practices in soil acidification constraint management have revealed several challenges, including fragmented knowledge systems, high technical thresholds, and pronounced regional disparities in technical capacity, which collectively hinder the systematic integration and dissemination of management experience. To address these limitations, this study proposes a lightweight autonomous construction framework for a knowledge graph of soil acidification management based on large language model (LLM) agents. By introducing an "AI associative matrix" and a semantic expansion-retrieval mechanism, the framework enables the system to automatically infer related concepts and relationships from a small set of domain-specific keywords, thereby generating an initial ontology structure and knowledge graph schema for management tasks. In addition, a network protocol-based control strategy is incorporated to semantically parse publicly available governmental reports and monitoring data, facilitating automated processes such as entity recognition and relation extraction. At the system implementation level, a cloud-edge collaborative lightweight architecture is adopted to reduce computational requirements and improve usability. Through an empirical in-situ deployment and lightweight field-level testing conducted directly at the farm sites of Chengmai County, Hainan Province, this framework demonstrated a robust capacity to adapt to users with different technical backgrounds and regions with varying levels of resource input, while providing extensibility for the continuous integration of emerging technologies and updated policy regulations. Overall, this study offers a lightweight, user-friendly, and scalable intelligent approach for cultivated land quality improvement and agricultural ecological management.
