RGB–multispectral image registration and generative spectral reconstruction for UAV-based jujube orchard monitoring
Decentralized no-reentry access control for automated feeding in socially ranked livestock groups
abstract: Automated feeding in group-housed livestock must combine individualized ration delivery with reliable control of competition for a shared feeder. We develop and analyze a decentralized feeder-access controller for socially ranked groups in which an animal that enters the feeder is blocked from re-entry until the next session. The controller requires only observable feeder-entry events and does not rely on centralized scheduling, hierarchy estimation, or global state information. We model the feeder as a stochastic multi-agent access-control system with ration, capacity, and conflict constraints. Within the decentralized policy class considered, we show that the no-reentry rule is sufficient to make the desired operating regime absorbing and, under an autonomy requirement for unfed animals, unique. We then study transient performance by simulation as a function of interaction scope, responsiveness, and dominance advantage. Global interaction scope yields systematically faster convergence than local scope, and stronger reactivity and dominance accelerate convergence further. Across the tested range of group sizes, local scope is generally better summarized by concave power-type fits, whereas global scope is markedly flatter. Additional simulations show that removing the no-reentry rule sharply reduces feeder utilization and ration completion while increasing congestion and rank-level inequality. Within the model studied here, these results identify a simple and implementable control law for automated livestock feeders and provide a simulation framework for evaluating feeder-access policies in precision livestock systems, including digital-twin and robotic-farming applications.

title: Dual-channel fluorescence LiDAR system for the nondestructive 3D sensing of plant physiological status
Field validation of a strain-gauge sensing workflow for relative structural-response monitoring in a multi-tunnel greenhouse
abstract: Lightweight greenhouse structures are subjected to combined environmental actions, yet their actual structural behavior under field conditions remains insufficiently documented using synchronized sensor data. This study presents field validation of a strain-gauge monitoring workflow for relative structural response assessment in a full-scale multi-tunnel greenhouse. The monitoring campaign combined 20 Hz strain records with one-minute external climate variables. Because the gauges were not zeroed against a known unloaded reference condition, all strain histories were interpreted as relative variations referenced to the initial monitoring state. The workflow linked each strain record to the final gauge labels shown in the monitoring layout, performed signal-quality screening, synchronized strain and environmental records, and compared the gauges by structural family and position. The five-day validation retained 22 strain-gauge signals from pillar, horizontal-member, vertical-bar, and arch locations. The strongest associations were generally linked to internal temperature and solar radiation rather than to the wind-speed-squared proxy. A nocturnal wind-speed decrease under near-constant internal air temperature was retained as an event-specific illustration of localized vertical-bar response rather than as a general wind-load validation. These results show that strain-gauge monitoring can provide interpretable field evidence from working greenhouse structures if gauge location, baseline definition, and environmental coupling are treated explicitly. The proposed workflow provides a basis for longer-term monitoring campaigns and the future integration of greenhouse sensor data with structural modeling and decision-support tools.

title: Ai-driven autonomous laser-weeding robots for agriculture 5.0: A systematic review of perception, navigation, and closed-loop control systems
A novel grid-based canopy cover index for estimating FAPAR of maize canopy from UAV multispectral images
Assessing tree vigor in orchards using wood segmentation and depth-based flash simulation on side-view RGB images
abstract: Tree vigor is a fundamental trait for orchard management, yet traditional measurements like trunk circumference or biomass weighing are slow, tedious and often lack precision. This study introduces a high-throughput phenotyping method using side-view RGB imaging of leafless trees to estimate wood projected area in orchards. A dataset of 2,802 annotated image patches, covering a variety of species, tree training methods, camera geometries and lighting conditions, was built to train nnU-Net models to segment all foreground wood pixels. The background influence was minimized by simulating a flash effect on the images using depth maps estimated from available deep learning models. Estimation of pruned wood biomass in espalier orchards served as a use case for wood segmentation: difference in the wood projected surface area computed before and after pruning based on segmented images, was linearly correlated with field-measured pruned wood biomass. Results highlight flash simulation’s ability to produce a single model capable of segmenting images acquired under natural and controlled conditions with similar accuracy (F 1 -score ≈ 0.91). Standard RGB and RGB-Depth models generally performed worse, especially under natural light, due to confusion with the background and less efficient use of depth information, respectively. The projected surface area of pruned wood, obtained through segmentation, was then shown to be an accurate proxy for pruned wood biomass for espaliered apple trees (R 2 = 0.92) and, to a lesser extent, peach trees (R 2 = 0.61). This illustrates the value of RGB imaging and wood segmentation for assessing vigor and architectural traits in fruit trees.

title: GTWLSTM-Lag: A maize yield prediction framework integrating spatiotemporal autocorrelation
Study on a real-time seeding flow detection method and device based on the seed flow spiral discretisation mechanism
From visual perception to actionable information for autonomous harvesting robots: A review
abstract: Reliable harvesting requires visual information that remains useful for planning and execution. This review examines four complementary functions of harvesting robot perception: detection and segmentation (D), metric three-dimensional localization (L), pose and task-relevant geometry (P), and environment reconstruction (E). D identifies the target, L locates it in a metric coordinate frame, P supplies the geometry needed for approach and detachment, and E describes the surrounding scene and its spatial context. A complete harvesting process requires these functions to work together, although individual studies may cover only some of them. The review distinguishes complete-system evidence, harvesting-specific module evidence, and adjacent evidence, using reported configurations to show how these functions are combined. An actionability gate assesses target identity, coordinate consistency, task-relevant geometry, scene coverage, uncertainty, information age, and the downstream planning or control consumer. A three-level framework connects module performance with information retained across interfaces and with robot or field deployment. By making the perception-to-action pathway explicit, this review clarifies the visual information required at each decision interface, identifies evidence gaps, and provides an engineering basis for designing and evaluating deployable harvesting-robot systems.

title: Hierarchical deep reinforcement learning for dual-arm robotic pear blossom pollination in dense orchard environments
Real-time in-water fish biomass estimation from stereo bounding-box geometry without dense depth maps
abstract: In biomass estimation of in-water fish, a primary challenge is accurately estimating depth to reconstruct the physical dimensions of detected specimens. Conventional stereo methods struggle in underwater environments due to light reflections, homogeneous backgrounds, and optical artifacts, often failing to produce reliable disparity maps. This study presents StereoGeoBox, a practical alternative that estimates depth solely from the geometric correspondence of stereo bounding boxes detected by YOLO11. This eliminates the need to compute a full dense depth map, and the resulting physical dimensions are used as inputs to an XGBoost model for real-time fish weight estimation. We validate our approach using a newly collected longitudinal dataset of in-water tilapia spanning four growth stages (2, 3, 6, and 15 months) over a 15-month period, captured with both ZED X and FD stereo cameras, with ground-truth width, length, and weight obtained via manual measurement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that StereoGeoBox achieves the lowest or near-lowest MAD and MPAE values for fish length, width, and weight across most evaluated datasets compared with conventional stereo vision and learning-based depth estimation methods, while generating substantially fewer outliers. The method also maintains reasonable estimation accuracy under challenging aquaculture conditions, including illumination variations, oxygen bubbles, and turbidity. On a Jetson Thor platform with an FD camera, StereoGeoBox achieves 25.40 FPS at 28.2 ms latency with just 17.7 MB of GPU memory, demonstrating substantially higher computational efficiency than the evaluated full depth-map approaches. The complete system — integrating underwater stereo vision, edge computing, and a cloud-based monitoring dashboard — enables practical remote monitoring of fish growth, supporting more efficient aquaculture management.

title: Rotary tiller blades for wet cohesive soil: Performance prediction and multi-objective optimisation with SPO–BO–BPNN

Structure over sound: A free box count out-predicts in-hive acoustics for honey-bee colony strength
abstract: In-hive microphones are widely promoted for non-invasive estimation of honey-bee colony strength (frames of bees), and benchmarks report near-perfect accuracy. Whether that accuracy survives on unseen colonies and apiaries decides deployability. We re-analysed two open multi-sensor datasets, UrBAN (ten urban colonies) and MSPB (53 rural colonies at two apiaries), harmonised to a shared 20-feature acoustic space with in-hive temperature and humidity. Random forests and hierarchical mixed models were evaluated under progressively stricter validation, from random k -fold to leave-one-apiary-out and cross-dataset transfer, with the acoustic, environmental and structural contributions separated by ablation. Most of the reported skill is not acoustic. Under leave-one-apiary-out validation the acoustic features alone reach R 2 = 0.17 , in-hive temperature and humidity alone 0.56, and the beekeeper’s box count alone 0.71; the box count from the previous visit, fixed before the label existed, still reaches 0.42 alone and 0.55 with climate. Adding acoustics never improved accuracy materially under any configuration tested ( Δ R 2 between −0.12 and ＋0.02). The box count’s 90% conformal intervals keep near-nominal empirical coverage across apiaries, while those of the sensor model cover 70% of cases in one transfer direction and 99% in the other. In an exploratory cross-dataset comparison, limited by a 17-assessment audio-matched UrBAN sample, the box count transferred in both directions and the acoustic features in neither. A plausible reason is sensing geometry: the microphone sits in the bottom brood box, which barely varies, while almost all population variation is above it. The box count mixes physical capacity with management decisions. It is therefore a diagnostic baseline and not a measurement instrument, and the finding is that a single bottom-box microphone adds nothing to it, though acoustics retain value for other targets. The conclusion rests on the within-MSPB cross-apiary comparison and is limited to a single bottom-box microphone, the shared feature space and the frames-of-bees target.

title: Dynamic real-time detection of maize ear dehusking clearance rate based on deep learning and multi-object tracking
abstract: Real-time assessment of maize-ear dehusking clearance rate is important for monitoring harvesting quality, but dynamic harvesting conditions can cause missed detections, false positives, and duplicate counting due to background interference, target-scale variation, motion blur, and severe occlusion. This study presents a real-time dehusking-clearance-rate monitoring framework integrating object detection, multi-object tracking, and identity-based duplicate-aware counting. An improved You Only Look Once version 11 nano (YOLOv11n) detector, termed PPSE-YOLO, was constructed by incorporating a Partial Frequency Dynamic Convolution-based C3k2 module (PFD_C3k2), the Pyramid Sparse Transformer (PST), and a Separated and Enhancement Attention Module (SEAMHead). PFD_C3k2 improves frequency- and texture-related feature representation under background interference and motion blur, PST enhances selective multi-scale feature fusion for maize ears with different apparent sizes, and SEAMHead strengthens the representation of visible features under partial occlusion. BoT-SORT maintains target identities across consecutive frames, and the resulting trajectories are converted into unique counting events for continuous dehusking-clearance-rate estimation. PPSE-YOLO achieved a Precision of 92.7%, a Recall of 91.8%, and an mAP@0.5 of 95.5%, representing improvements of 2.4, 0.9, and 1.5 percentage points, respectively, over YOLOv11n. Meanwhile, its computational complexity and parameter count were reduced from 6.3 to 5.1 GFLOPs and from 2.58 to 2.28 M, respectively. BoT-SORT achieved an MOTA of 92.05% and an IDF1 of 89.87%. At the system level, the framework achieved an overall counting consistency of 97.67%, a mean absolute dehusking-clearance-rate estimation error of 2.02 percentage points across 10 test groups, and an average end-to-end processing speed of 34 FPS. These results indicate the feasibility of the framework for real-time maize dehusking monitoring under the tested harvesting conditions.

title: Spatially optimized chlorophyll fluorescence imaging for early detection of soft rot in Napa cabbage
FluxMate: An off-grid, cost-effective and dual-mode automated chamber system to monitor carbon dioxide fluxes in grassland ecosystems
abstract: Measuring greenhouse gas (GHG) fluxes in an ecosystem is essential to assess their contribution to global warming. Automated chamber systems can capture high-frequency data to estimate GHG fluxes. An automated dual-mode stand-alone chamber system was developed to measure carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) fluxes in agricultural ecosystems. The array mode consists of several chambers connected via tubing to a research-grade analyser, whereas the independent chamber mode consists of low-cost sensors inside each chamber. Both modes calculate fluxes, measure environmental conditions, and record images of the vegetation inside the chambers to calculate vegetation indices. The low-cost sensors showed a reliable estimation of CO 2 concentration against a research-grade gas analyser (MAPE < 22.1%, RMSE < 25 ppm, CCC > 0.96) and CO 2 fluxes (CCC = 0.97, R 2 > 0.94, with an average RMSE of 4.04 and MAE of 2.48 kg CO 2 ha hr -1 ). Furthermore, CO 2 fluxes followed diurnal patterns similar to the research-grade analyser, with CO 2 uptake during the daytime and release during nighttime. On average, CO 2 fluxes from the sensors underestimated fluxes by 10.7% compared to the research-grade analyser, with minimal systematic linear deviation from the 1:1 line (C.b > 0.99) and 95% of the error being random. Overall, the independent automated chamber system introduced in this study can measure CO 2 fluxes at a lower cost and with a more flexible approach compared to the research-grade analyser because individual chambers do not need to be connected to an analyser. Independently, low-cost chamber systems could allow scaling up measurements and replications of fluxes in agricultural systems.

title: MCAFNet: A multimodal audio-visual cross-attention fusion network for on-the-branch durian (Durio zibethinus L.) fruit maturity assessment
Active disturbance control system and optimized algorithm for rotational-speed stability using a developed horticulture electric direct-drive rotary tiller
Predicting and mapping stem water potential in walnut orchards using machine learning, geostatistics, and spatial validation
abstract: Midday stem water potential (SWP) is a widely used indicator of orchard water status, but pressure-chamber measurements are labor intensive and spatially sparse. This study evaluated machine-learning and spatial-statistical approaches using repeated measurements from 30 trees at 10 monitoring sites during 2019–2021. Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and a stacked ensemble used ETo, vapor pressure deficit (VPD), air temperature, soil temperature, solar radiation, wind speed, Easting, and Northing as predictors. Strict leave-one-site-out (Site-LOSO) validation was the primary test of transfer to an unmonitored site. RF had the highest pooled Site-LOSO point estimate (R 2 = 0.41, RMSE = 0.21 MPa, MAE = 0.16 MPa), followed by the ensemble (R 2 = 0.38, RMSE = 0.22 MPa) and XGBoost (R 2 = 0.37, RMSE = 0.22 MPa). Same-date field-assisted inverse-distance weighting achieved R 2 = 0.39 and RMSE = 0.22 MPa. RF reproduced monitored-network date means well (R 2 = 0.97; RMSE = 0.03 MPa) but not within-date spatial anomalies at withheld sites (R 2 = − 0.12; r = 0.09), and leave-one-year-out transfer was weak. The fitted models were applied over canopy pixels for 11 Ceres acquisition dates in 2020. All model maps were spatially smooth at the native grid, but their spatial patterns and within-map variation differed among algorithms and dates. Residual spatial dependence, heterogeneous tree-level performance, and mixed same-date checks indicate substantial uncertainty in fine-scale spatial transfer. The 0.5-m grid is a model-output support and not an independently validated SWP measurement resolution.

title: IoT-Enabled precision fertigation for Ngoc Linh ginseng house Cultivation: Hydraulic–Electronic Co-Design and Edge–Gateway validation
Selective harvesting apple quality assessment in modern orchards: Fruit surface defect detection and severity analysis
Image segmentation of sugarcane plants using u-net architecture and pre-trained deep learning models
abstract: Gap identification in the sugarcane ( Saccharum officinarum spp) is important because the uniformity of germination is highly correlated with yield. Field-scale spatial image segmentation using drone imagery to clearly distinguish sugarcane from other materials in the field facilitates a better understanding of gaps and the reasons behind their occurrence. This research reports on the use of this approach to investigate segmentation of sugarcane imagery using six pre-trained transfer learning models and a proposed U-Net model for this purpose. The pre-trained models selected for this study were VGG19, ResNet50, InceptionV3, InceptionResNetV2, MobileNetV2 and EfficientNetB7. Model performance metrics such as model accuracy, loss function, F1-score, Dice loss, IoU, and Jaccard loss were used to evaluate the models. The dataset used in this study was RGB imagery captured from a drone. Ground-truth data consisted of 317 masked images (full rows of sugarcane, incomplete rows of sugarcane, and no sugarcane) for training and validating the model. The resultant models were used to perform spatial image segmentation on a proof-of-concept area. Of the models evaluated, five achieved high levels of spatial image segmentation for sugarcane. From a resource constraint, the proposed U-Net model, VGG19, and InceptionV3 generated the most suitable models for sugarcane segmentation. VGG19 resulted in the best performance scores with accuracy 0.893 but was not substantially different from the proposed U-Net and InceptionV3 models. When processing time and available resources were taken into account, InceptionV3 was also found to be a suitable alternative. Therefore, we conclude that image segmentation of sugarcane plants using the VGG19 and InceptionV3 architectures is a suitable choice for this type of application. These algorithms enable clear visualization of the emerging sugarcane plants, allowing them to be distinguished from the other in the row and across the field. Ultimately, this will be of benefit for future research that can help sugarcane farmers plan and make prompt decisions about field activities to achieve sustainable sugarcane farming, including future studies to identify the causes of the gaps in sugarcane rows.

title: Editorial Board
A unified modeling framework for tree root characterization and scaling: Method in belowground ecology and evolution
abstract: Conventional ecological modeling and sampling frameworks frequently rely on a binary, isolated fine-root paradigm (e.g., a strict 2-mm diameter threshold) that treats fine roots as functionally homogeneous. This approach obscures the full structural aggregation patterns, emergent network complexity, and multi-scale scaling properties of root systems. To address these limitations, this study developed an irregular cylinder ( IC ) root model within a unified structural architecture framework. Tree root networks were modeled as hierarchical clusters of irregular cylinders governed by stable, long-axis orthographic 2D quadrilateral polygon shape constraints to facilitate systematic sampling, digital image processing, and cross-scale annotation. The framework was evaluated using empirical datasets compiled from Cunninghamia lanceolata across various forest developmental stages. The results demonstrate significant non-linear variations in size scaling ratios and scaling exponents, indicating a highly assembled branching architecture with pronounced structural redundancy rather than taproot dominance. Specifically, fine roots, absorptive roots, and second-order roots exhibited distinct shrinkage effects, with scaling exponents for total length, surface area, and volume decreasing sequentially as trait dimensionality increased. Maximum efficiency of nutrient absorption“ is inconsistent with the classic metabolic scaling model. Crucially, the established six-order diameter size classifier successfully reconciles conflicting traditional, functional, and order-based root definitions, serving as a reliable cross-scale operator. By integrating 3D phenotyping, recursive topological constraints, and functional scaling, this modeling framework provides a reproducible mechanism to bridge static structural traits with dynamic developmental processes. These advancements offer a rigorous foundation for refining belowground resource allocation parameterizations in dynamic terrestrial biosphere models (TBMs) under changing climate scenarios.

title: Explainability-guided transformer-based anomaly screening in agave crops

Non-contact backfat thickness prediction in finishing pigs via multimodal feature fusion for pig sorting systems
Forecasting drought across Canada using a hybrid machine learning approach: a national perspective for adaptations and early warning systems
abstract: Drought is a major natural hazard in Canada, with significant socio-economic impacts across the country’s diverse climatic and geographic regions. This study proposes a hybrid forecasting framework that combines fast adaptive empirical mode decomposition (FAEMD), an ensemble deep random vector functional link (edRVFL) network, and the energy valley optimizer (EVO) to model nonstationary hydrological time series. Using 74 years (1951–2024) of meteorological data from 24 Canadian meteorological stations, we first identified substantial spatial variability and nonstationary trends in historical drought conditions. The proposed FAEMD-edRVFL-EVO framework was then used to forecast the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI 12 ) at one-, two-, and three-month lead times and compared against standalone and hybrid implementations of extreme gradient boosting, random forest, and k -nearest neighbor algorithms. FAEMD-edRVFL-EVO consistently achieved the best performance, with median correlation coefficients of 0.999, 0.980, and 0.906 for one-, two-, and three-month forecasts, respectively. Performance remained strong in climatically complex regions, particularly in Western and Northern Canada. By effectively isolating nonstationary signals, this applied study demonstrates that the integrated pipeline provides a scalable, accurate, and computationally efficient practical solution for large-scale drought forecasting and early warning under increasing climatic uncertainty.

title: A robotic lotus pod picking method integrating key point detection and active viewpoint adjustment: experimental validation under controlled laboratory conditions
PRIM3: pod reconstruction and instance matching in 3D for lima bean pod counting and yield assessment
Estimating and Forecasting Grapevine Phenology using Deep Learning and Mechanistic models: A comparative study
abstract: Accurate monitoring of key phenological stages, such as bud-break, blooming, veraison, and berries ripe, is essential for optimizing vineyard management, especially in the context of climate change. Grapevine phenology, primarily driven by temperature, has been extensively studied with the most common prediction methods based on the growing-degree-days (GDD) approach. In this paper we propose and compare two novel methodologies, respectively based on a mechanistic and a deep learning approach, to detect and forecast key phenological stages. The mechanistic model simulates the effects of both air temperature and water availability on the major plant metabolic processes that drive the annual phenological cycle (vegetative and reproductive growth, and sugar accumulation in the berry), whereas the deep learning model, based on a Recurrent Neural Network, infers directly the phenological cycle taking as input the time series of the daily weather station measurements. Using seven years of phenological data collected from five grape varieties (‘Aglianico’, ‘Greco’ ‘Syrah’, ‘Touriga Franca’, and ‘Touriga Nacional’) across four Mediterranean sites in Italy, Spain, and Portugal, we evaluate the performance of these models against traditional GDD-based methods. Cross-validation results show that while the mechanistic model excels at predicting bud-break, with a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 4.9 days compared to 5.7 and 5.6 days of the GDD-based and the deep learning model, respectively, the deep learning model is an all-around optimal methodology in terms of predicting accuracy across different stages, resulting in an overall MAE slightly under 5 days, with an average error reduction of 0.6 to 1.6 days respect to the two GDD-based models tested. Furthermore, we illustrate how these models can leverage sub-seasonal weather forecasts to predict phenological events in advance, offering practical tools for vineyard managers. This was particularly true for the deep learning model, that was able to predict grapevine phenological stages two weeks in advance with an average error lower than 6 days. These findings highlight the potential of these novel approaches for automating phenology monitoring and improving decision-making in viticulture under changing climate conditions.

title: GAN-diffusion hybrids for image generation in smart agriculture: A systematic review
Linking video tracks and RFID identification to monitor individual broilers in group housing
abstract: Monitoring an individual broiler’s movement, interactions, and environment using video and RFID allows breeders to identify novel or indicator traits of their health, welfare, and performance, potentially improving the effectiveness of selection. However, video monitoring and identifying multiple, similar-looking, group-housed broilers is difficult. This study developed and investigated a data-fusion approach integrating video tracking with RFID identification to reconstruct individual broiler trajectories in group housing. Thirty-nine RFID-tagged broilers were recorded in a pen with thirty subfloor RFID antennas and a video camera at 18 days of age. Tracking was achieved with a YOLOv7-tiny model and a modified version of SORT. Tracks were linked to RFID-tags either through a direct approach or through the developed two-step approach consisting of location estimation through a Hidden Markov Model (HMM), with or without incorporating additional video information, and trajectory reconstruction using a greedy algorithm. Four antenna configurations were assessed: full-grid (#30), two-lines (#12), cross-pattern (#10), and two-antenna (#2). In all antenna configurations, the developed approach outperformed the direct approach, with lower average positions errors and less missing positions when evaluated against ground-truth positions [mean (SD)]: 0.021(0.10) vs. 0.48(0.54), 0.14(0.30) vs. 0.71(0.61), 0.30(0.45) vs. 0.69(0.50) and 0.85(0.59) vs. 1.03(0.60) m, respectively. The developed sensor data-fusion approach provides individual trajectories of group-housed broilers for subsequent locomotion phenotyping (such as distance walked, speed, and acceleration) by combining the spatial precision of video with the identification reliability of RFID.

Pre-symptomatic crop intelligence: a closed-loop framework for anticipatory, confidence-aware decision-making in site-specific crop protection
abstract: Abstract Purpose Symptom-triggered crop protection acts only after damage is committed, and the intervention window has narrowed. This review reframes pre-symptomatic sensing from a detection problem into a closed decision loop, establishing the physiological lead time of a signal, set against its detection confidence and the latency of the response it can trigger, as the organizing principle for anticipatory, site-specific decision-making. Methods A systematic-narrative synthesis was conducted across major bibliographic databases through June 2026. Studies reporting pre-symptomatic capability under field or realistic conditions were retained and coded onto a coupled lead-time × confidence × actionability framework spanning sensing, inference, and actuation. Results Optical modalities were found to dominate the evidence base, while electrophysiological and volatile signals extended achievable lead time. Single modalities were insufficient to separate biotic from abiotic stress, motivating heterogeneous fusion. Edge inference and temporal onset forecasting remained immature, detection confidence was rarely quantified, and the sensing-to-actuation loop was seldom closed. Reported performance degraded sharply from laboratory to field, particularly in perennial and smallholder systems. Conclusions A unifying Pre-Symptomatic Crop Intelligence framework is proposed, governed by the principle that system value is bounded by the weakest of lead time, detection confidence, and response latency; priorities identified include lead-time-labeled benchmarks, uncertainty-aware inference, field-robust fusion, and economic evaluation for perennial crops.
